column2: Borrowed from Afrikaans aardvark (now rare), erdvark, from aarde (“earth”, from Middle Dutch aerde) + vark (“pig”, from Middle Dutch varken). Early European colonists in South Africa noticed that the animal was similar to a pig, while aarde hints at the animal's habit of burrowing.
column3: noun. The nocturnal, insectivorous, burrowing mammal Orycteropus afer, of the order Tubulidentata and somewhat resembling a pig. Common in some parts of sub-Saharan Africa.

column2: From ab- + normal. First attested in 1835, replacing the earlier anormal and even earlier abnormous, from Latin abnormis (“departing from normal”), from either ab- (“away from”) + norma (“rule, norm”), or Ancient Greek ἀνώμαλος (anṓmalos).
column3: adjective. Not conforming to rule or system; deviating from the usual or normal type.

column2: First attested around 1380. From Middle English absolut, from Middle French absolut, from Latin absolūtus (“unconditional; unfettered; completed”), perfect passive participle of absolvō (“loosen, set free, complete”), from ab (“away”) + solvo (“to loose”). Influenced in part by Old French absolu. Compare absolve.
column3: adjective. Free of restrictions, limitations, qualifications or conditions; unconditional. Unrestricted by laws, a constitution, or parliamentary or judicial or other checks; (legally) unlimited in power, especially if despotic. Characteristic of an absolutist ruler: domineering, peremptory.

column2: From absorb + -ed.
column3: adjective. Fully occupied with one's thoughts; engrossed.

column2: From Middle English abstract, borrowed from Latin abstractus, perfect passive participle of abstrahō (“draw away”), formed from abs- (“away”) + trahō (“to pull, draw”). The verbal sense is first attested in 1542.
column3: noun. An abridgement or summary of a longer publication.

column2: From both the Medieval Latin acadēmicus and the French académique, from Latin academia, from Ancient Greek ἀκαδημικός (akadēmikós), from Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía) or Ἀκαδήμεια (Akadḗmeia), the name of the place where Plato taught; compare academy. By surface analysis, academy + -ic.
column3: adjective. Belonging to the school or philosophy of Plato.

column2: From accept + -ed.
column3: verb. simple past and past participle of accept

column2: First attested in the late 14th century. From Middle English accident, from Old French accident, from Latin accidēns, present active participle of accidō (“happen”); from ad (“to”) + cadō (“fall”). See cadence, case. In the sense “unintended pregnancy”, first attested in 1932.
column3: noun. An unexpected event with negative consequences occurring without the intention of the one suffering the consequences, and (in the strict sense) not directly caused by humans.

column2: Borrowed from Latin accūrātus, perfect passive participle of accūrō (“to take care of”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + cūrō (“care for”). First attested in 1610. Compare English cure.
column3: adjective. Telling the truth or giving a true result; exact; not defective or faulty.

column2: The verb is from Middle English accustomen, from Old French acoustumer, acustumer (Modern French accoutumer) corresponding to a (“to, toward”) + custom. More at custom, costume. The noun is from Middle English acustom.
column3: verb. To make familiar by use; to cause to accept; to habituate, familiarize, or inure.

column2: Borrowed from Medieval Latin acousticus, acūsticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκουστῐκός (akoustĭkós, “of or for hearing”), from ἀκούω (akoúō, “to hear”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, adjectival suffix).
column3: adjective. Pertaining to the sense of hearing, the organs of hearing, or the science of sounds.

column2: From active + -ate.
column3: verb. To encourage development or induce increased activity; to stimulate.

column2: From late Middle English actyvely; equivalent to active + -ly.
column3: adverb. In an active manner.

column2: From Middle French activité, from Latin activitas. Equivalent to active + -ity.
column3: noun. The state or quality of being active; activeness.

column2: From Middle English actually, actuelly, equivalent to actual + -ly.
column3: adverb. In act or in fact; really; in truth; positively.

column2: Sense of “what is added” dates from 14th century, from Middle English addicioun, addition, from Old French adition, from Latin additiōnem, accusative singular of additiō, from addō (“add, put”).
column3: noun. The act of adding anything.

column2: Learned borrowing from Latin adaequātus, perfect passive participle of adaequō (“to make equal to”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from ad (“to, towards, at”) + aequō (“to make equal, equalize”), from aequus (“equal”). Cognate with French adéquat. By surface analysis, ad- + equate.
column3: adjective. Equal to or fulfilling some requirement.

column2: From Middle English *adherynge, adherande, present participle of Middle English *adheren, from Old French *adherer, aderer and Medieval Latin adhaereō (“adhere”, verb), equivalent to adhere + -ing.
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of adhere

column2: Borrowed from Latin adiacēns, adiacentis, derivative of adiaceō (“to lie beside”); from ad (“to”) + iaceō (“to lie down”).
column3: adjective. Lying next to, close, or contiguous; neighboring; bordering on.

column2: Borrowed from French adoption, from Latin adoptio, allied to adoptare (“to adopt”). Equivalent to adopt + -ion.
column3: noun. The act of adopting.

column2: From advance + -ed.
column3: verb. simple past and past participle of advance

column2: From advise + -ory.
column3: adjective. Able to give advice.

column2: From Middle English advocat, advoket, from Old French advocat, from Latin advocātus (“an advocate”), from the substantivization of the perfect passive participle of advocāre (“to call for”) (see -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from a calque of Ancient Greek παράκλητος (paráklētos) (whence English paraclete). Doublet of advoke, avocat, avouch, and avow. The verb derives from the noun on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix).
column3: noun. Someone whose job is to speak for someone's case in a court of law; a counsel.

column2: From agree + -ing.
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of agree

column2: From air + -craft.
column3: noun. A vehicle capable of atmospheric flight due to interaction with the air, such as buoyancy or lift.

column2: From allergy + -ic.
column3: adjective. Of or pertaining to allergy.

column2: From Middle English alliaunce, from Old French aliance (French alliance). Equivalent to ally + -ance. Compare with Doric Greek ἁλία (halía, “assembly”). See also al-.
column3: noun. The state of being allied.

column2: From Latin allocātus, perfect passive participle of Latin allocō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ad- (“to”) + locō. Doublet of allow. By surface analysis, al- + locate.
column3: verb. To set aside for a purpose.

column2: Doublet of alfabeto. Dipslaced native Old English stæfrǣw (literally " staff - row ").
column3: noun. The set of letters used when writing in a language.

column2: From Middle English althagh, from Old English compound of eall (“all (emphatic)”) + þēah (“though”). By surface analysis, al(l) + though.
column3: conjunction. Though, even though, in spite of or despite the fact that: introducing a clause that expresses a concession.

column2: Equivalent to ana- (“functionally similar”) + -logue. See analog.
column3: adjective. Alternative spelling of analog.

column2: See analysis.
column3: noun. plural of analysis

column2: From Medieval Latin analysis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλυσις (análusis), from ἀναλύω (analúō, “to unravel, investigate”), from ἀνα- (ana-, “thoroughly”) + λύω (lúō, “to loosen”).
column3: noun. Decomposition into components in order to study (a complex thing, concept, theory, etc.).

column2: From Middle English ancestre, auncestre, ancessour; the first forms from Old French ancestre (modern French ancêtre), from the Latin nominative antecessor (“one who goes before”); the last form from Old French ancessor, from Latin antecessōrem, accusative of antecessor, from antecēdō (“to go before”) + -tor (“-er”), from ante- (“before”) + cēdō (“to go”). See cede, and compare with antecessor.
column3: noun. One from whom a person is descended, whether on the father's or mother's side, at any distance of time; a progenitor; a forefather; a forebear.

column2: Late 17 c., from French anecdote, from Ancient Greek ἀνέκδοτος (anékdotos, “accounts unpublished”), from ἀν- (an-, “not, un-”) + ἔκδοτος (ékdotos, “published”), from ἐκδίδωμι (ekdídōmi, “I publish”), from ἐκ- (ek-, “out”) + δίδωμι (dídōmi, “I give”). Virtually identical cognates in other European languages – French anecdote, German Anekdote, Spanish anécdota, among others.
column3: noun. A short account of a real incident or person, often humorous or interesting.

column2: From Old French anoncier, from Latin annūntiāre, from ad + nūntiō (“report, relate”), from nūntius (“messenger, bearer of news”). See nuncio. Doublet of annunciate. See also an-.
column3: verb. To give public notice of, especially for the first time; to make known.

column2: From annoy + -ing.
column3: adjective. Causing irritation or annoyance; troublesome; vexatious.

column2: From annual + -ly.
column3: adverb. Once every year without fail, yearly

column2: From Latin antidotum, from Ancient Greek ἀντίδοτον (antídoton, “antidote, remedy”), Clipping of ἀντίδοτον φάρμακον (antídoton phármakon, “drug given against”), from ἀντιδίδωμι (antidídōmi, “to give in return, repay”), from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + δίδωμι (dídōmi, “to give”). Compare French antidote.
column3: noun. A remedy to counteract the effects of poison.

column2: From any + place.
column3: adverb. At a non-specific place; anywhere.

column2: From Middle English anything, enything, onything, from Late Old English aniþing, from earlier ǣniġ þing (literally “any thing”), equivalent to any + thing.
column3: pronoun. Any object, act, state, event, or fact whatsoever; a thing of any kind; something or other.

column2: From any + where.
column3: adverb. In or at any location.

column2: From appall + -ed.
column3: adjective. Shocked, horrified by something unpleasant.

column2: From Middle English apparaunt, aparaunt, from Old French aparent, aparant, in turn from Latin appārēns, appārentis, present participle of appāreō.
column3: adjective. Capable of being seen, or easily seen; open to view; visible to the eye; within sight or view.

column2: Borrowed from Latin appendix.
column3: noun. Something attached to something else; an attachment or accompaniment.

column2: From Latin applausus, from applaudō (“to strike against, to applaud”) (whence applaud).
column3: noun. The act of applauding; approbation and praise publicly expressed by the clapping of hands, stamping or tapping of the feet, acclamation, huzzas, or other means; marked commendation.

column2: From Middle English aprochen, borrowed from Old French aprochier (modern French approcher), from Late Latin appropiāre, a verb based on Latin prope (“near”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pro- (a variant of *per- (“before, in front; first”)) + *-kʷe (“suffix forming distributives from interrogatives”)).
column3: verb. To come or go near, in place or time; to move toward; to advance nearer; to draw nigh.

column2: From approve + -al.
column3: noun. An expression granting permission; an indication of agreement with a proposal; an acknowledgement that a person, thing, or event meets requirements.

column2: From argue + -able.
column3: adjective. That can be argued; that can be proven or strongly supported with sound logical deduction, precedent, and evidence.

column2: From arguable + -ly.
column3: adverb. As can be supported or proven by sound logical deduction, evidence, and precedent, but without absolute certainty.

column2: From Middle English argument, from Anglo-Norman and Old French arguement, from Latin argumentum. The English word is analysable as argue + -ment. Doublet of argumentum. Displaced native Old English racu and ġeflit.
column3: noun. A fact or statement used to support a proposition; a reason.

column2: From Middle English arrogaunt, from Old French arrogant, from Latin arrogāns, present active participle of arrogō.
column3: adjective. Having excessive pride in oneself, often with contempt or disrespect for others.

column2: Borrowed from French artistique, from artiste + -ique. By surface analysis, artist + -ic.
column3: adjective. Having or revealing creative skill.

column2: From Middle English assemblen, from Old French assembler (“to assemble”), from Medieval Latin assimulāre (“to bring together”), from ad- + simulō (“copy, imitate”), from similis (“like, similar”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”). Doublet of assimilate.
column3: verb. To put together.

column2: From Middle English assemblee, from Anglo-Norman asemblee (Old French asemblee, French assemblée). By surface analysis, assemble + -y.
column3: noun. A set of pieces that work together in unison as a mechanism or device.

column2: The noun is derived from Middle English asterisk [and other forms], from Late Latin asteriscus (“asterisk; small star”), from Ancient Greek ἀστερῐ́σκος (asterĭ́skos, “asterisk; small star”), from ᾰ̓στήρ (ăstḗr, “celestial body (star, planet, and other lights in the sky such as meteors)”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs- (“to burn; to glow”)) + -ῐ́σκος (-ĭ́skos, diminutive suffix). Doublet of asteriscus and piecewise doublet of starrish. Noun sense 1.1.2 (“something which is of little importance or which is marginal”) refers to the use of an asterisk to denote a footnote or marginal note in a text; in other words, information that is not important enough to be incorporated into the main text. Noun sense 1.1.3 (“blemish in an otherwise outstanding achievement”) refers to the use of an asterisk in a sporting record to indicate that the record is qualified in some manner (for example, that the sportsperson was found to have taken performance-enhancing drugs at the time). The verb is derived from the noun.
column3: noun. A small star; also, something resembling or shaped like a star. The star-shaped symbol *, which is used in printing and writing for various purposes, including to refer a reader to a note at the bottom of a page or in a margin, and to indicate the omission of letters or words; a star. Something resembling or shaped like an asterisk symbol. Something which is of little importance or which is marginal; a footnote. A blemish in an otherwise outstanding achievement.

column2: From French attitude, from Italian attitudine (“attitude, aptness”), from Medieval Latin aptitūdō (“aptitude”) and actitūdō (“acting, posture”), from Latin aptō and actitō. Doublet of aptitude.
column3: noun. The position of the body or way of carrying oneself.

column2: From Middle English attourne, from Old French atorné, past participle of atorner, atourner, aturner (“to attorn”), in the sense of "one appointed or constituted".
column3: noun. A lawyer; one who advises or represents others in legal matters as a profession.

column2: From Middle English audience, from Middle French audience, from Old French audience, from Latin audientia, from present participle audiēns (“hearing”), from verb audiō (“to hear”). Doublet of audiencia.
column3: noun. A group of people within hearing; specifically, a large gathering of people listening to or watching a performance, speech, etc.

column2: Back-formation from automation.
column3: verb. To replace or enhance human labor with machines.

column2: From Middle English bakbon, bakebon, bac-bon; equivalent to back + bone. Compare the semantically analogous English ridgebone.
column3: noun. The series of vertebrae, separated by disks, that encloses and protects the spinal cord, and runs down the middle of the back in vertebrate animals.

column2: From Middle English bakwarde, abakward, equivalent to back (adverb) + -ward. Cognate with Old Frisian bekward (“backward”).
column3: adjective. Indicating position or direction. Situated toward or at the rear of something.

column2: Borrowed from New Latin bacteria, plural of bactērium, from Ancient Greek βακτήριον (baktḗrion, “little rod”); by surface analysis, bacteri(um) + -a.
column3: noun. plural of bacterium

column2: Partial calque of Italian bancarotta (literally “a broken bench”), from banca (“bank”, literally “bench”) + rotta (“broken, rupted”), which refers to an out-of-business bank, having its bench physically broken, signifying that the working moneylender was insolvent.
column3: adjective. In a condition of bankruptcy; unable to pay outstanding debts or meet financial obligations; specifically, having been legally declared insolvent.

column2: From base + -ment.
column3: noun. A floor of a building below ground level. Ellipsis of semi-basement, a floor mostly below grade

column2: From bath + room. Compare Dutch badkamer (“bathroom”), German Badezimmer (“bathroom”), Swedish badrum (“bathroom”), Faroese baðrúm (“bathroom”).
column3: noun. A room containing a shower or bathtub, and a toilet.

column2: From Middle English begynner, equivalent to begin + -er. Cognate with West Frisian begjinner (“beginner”), Dutch beginner (“beginner”), Low German begünner (“beginner”), Danish nybegynder (“beginner, novice”, literally “new-beginner”).
column3: noun. Someone who is just starting at something, or has only recently started.

column2: From Middle English behavoure, behaver, from behaven (modern behave), morphologically equivalent to behave + -ior. The suffix was adopted in imitation of havour (modern haviour, havior), an etymologically unrelated word that was corrupted from Anglo‐Norman Anglo-Norman aveir and Old French Old French avoir (“property, wealth”) through false association with the native English verb have. The French term derives ultimately from Latin Latin habēre (“to have, hold”). Compare Scots havings (“behavior”), from have (“to behave”). Replaced Old English ġebǣru.
column3: noun. Human conduct relative to social norms.

column2: From Middle English bilevar, bileever, belever, equivalent to believe + -er.
column3: noun. A person who believes; especially regarding religion.

column2: From Medieval Latin biblicus + English -al, equivalent to bible + -ical.
column3: adjective. Of or relating to the Bible.

column2: From bill + fold.
column3: noun. A small, folding sleeve or case designed to hold paper currency, as well as credit cards, pictures, etc.

column2: From Middle English birthdai, birtheday, from Old English ġebyrddæġ (“birthday”), influenced by Old Norse burðr, equivalent to birth + day. Compare Saterland Frisian Gebuursdai (“birthday”), Dutch geboortedag (“birthday”), Low German Geboortsdag (“birthday”), German Geburtstag (“birthday”), Norwegian bursdag, gebursdag (“birthday”). Eclipsed non-native Middle English nativitee (“birth, nativity, birthday”), from Old French nativité, nativited, from Latin nātīvitas.
column3: noun. The anniversary of the day on which someone is born.

column2: From Middle English blastynge, equivalent to blast + -ing (present participle ending).
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of blast

column2: From Middle English blessinge, blessynge, from Old English blētsung, blēdsung (“a blessing”), equivalent to bless + -ing.
column3: noun. Some kind of divine or supernatural aid, or reward.

column2: From book + shop.
column3: noun. A shop that sells books.

column2: From bound + -ary.
column3: noun. The dividing line or location between two areas.

column2: From breathe + -ed.
column3: verb. simple past and past participle of breathe

column2: From Middle English breedyng, bredynge (“gestation, incubation, propagation, hatching; engineering, formation, development, growth”), equivalent to breed + -ing.
column3: noun. Propagation of offspring through sexual reproduction.

column2: From Early Modern English brethren, plural of brother, from Middle English brethren, from Middle English brethere, brether + -en (plural ending). Ultimately from Old English brōþor, brōþru (“brothers, brethren”), influenced by Old English brēþer, dative singular of brōþor (“brother”). Equivalent to brother + -en (plural ending). Compare German Brüder (“brothers, brethren”). More at brother. The vowel change (from o to e) is called umlaut.
column3: noun. plural of brother

column2: From Middle English brightliche, from Old English beorhtlice, equivalent to bright + -ly.
column3: adverb. In a bright manner.

column2: From Middle English byldynge, buyldyng, byldyng, buldynge, buldyng, boldyng, equivalent to build + -ing. Compare also related Middle English bold (“edifice, castle, mansion”), from Old English bold (“building, dwelling, house”).
column3: noun. The act or process by which something is built; construction.

column2: Borrowed from French bulletin. By surface analysis, bull (“ball”) + -et (“diminutive”) + -in (“diminutive”).
column3: noun. A short report, especially one released through official channels to be immediately broadcast or publicized.

column2: From Middle English busines, busynes, businesse, bisynes, from Old English bisiġnes (“business, busyness”), equivalent to busy + -ness. Doublet of busyness. Sense 17 (something very good, top quality), possibly derives from " the bee's knees "
column3: noun. A specific commercial enterprise or establishment.

column2: Borrowed from French caféine, from café (“coffee”), or German Caffein, Kaffein (cp. Coffein, Koffein), from Kaffee (“coffee”) (cp. Kaffe, Koffee, Koffe), or Italian caffè (“coffee”) + -ine.
column3: noun. An alkaloid, C 8 H 10 N 4 O 2, found naturally in tea and coffee plants, which acts as a mild stimulant on the central nervous system.

column2: From Middle English kalender, from Old French calendier, from Latin calendarium (“account book”), from kalendae (“the first day of the month”), from kalō (“to announce solemnly, to call out (the sighting of the new moon)”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁-. Doublet of calendarium. Displaced native Old English rīmbōc and ġerīmbōc.
column3: noun. Any system by which time is divided into days, weeks, months, and years.

column2: From French campagne, from Italian campagna (“field, military operation”), from Late Latin campānia (“open country, battlefield”), from Latin campus (“field”). Doublet of campania, campagna, and champagne.
column3: noun. A series of operations undertaken to achieve a set goal.

column2: From Middle English capacite, from Old French capacite, from Latin capācitās (whence -acity), from capāx (“able to hold much”), from capiō (“to hold, to contain, to take, to understand”).
column3: noun. The ability to hold, receive, or absorb.

column2: From Middle English careles, from Old English carlēas (“careless, reckless, void of care, free from care, free”), equivalent to care + -less. Cognate with Icelandic kærulaus (“careless, negligent”).
column3: adjective. Not concerned or worried (about).

column2: From Middle English cariage, from Old Northern French cariage, from carier (“to carry”).
column3: noun. The act of conveying; carrying.

column2: Borrowed from French cassette.
column3: noun. A small flat case containing magnetic tape on two reels, used to record and play back audio and video material.

column2: Late Middle English, borrowed from French catégorie, from Middle French categorie, from Late Latin catēgoria (“class of predicables”), from Ancient Greek κατηγορία (katēgoría, “head of predicables”). Doublet of categoria.
column3: noun. A group, often named or numbered, to which items are assigned based on similarity or defined criteria.

column2: From Old French catholique, from Latin catholicus, from Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós, “universal”), from κατά (katá, “according to”) + ὅλος (hólos, “whole”).
column3: adjective. Universal; all-encompassing.

column2: From New Latin cellulāris, from cellula (“cell”) + -āris.
column3: adjective. Of, relating to, consisting of, or resembling a cell or cells.

column2: From Middle English cerymonye, from Latin caerimonia or caeremonia, later often cerimonia (“sacredness, reverence, a sacred rite”).
column3: noun. A ritual, with religious or cultural significance.

column2: From chair + -man.
column3: noun. A person presiding over a meeting, sometimes especially a man.

column2: From Middle English champioun, from Old French champion, from Medieval Latin campio (“combatant in a duel, champion”), from Frankish *kampijō (“fighter”), from Proto-West Germanic *kampijō (“combat soldier”), a derivative of *kampijan (“to battle, to campaign”), itself a derivative of *kamp (“battlefield, battle”), ultimately a borrowing in West-Germanic from Latin campus (“a field, a plain, a place of action”). Cognate with Old English cæmpa, cempa (“soldier, warrior, champion”), Old High German kempfeo, kempfo (“fighter, warrior, champion”), whence archaic German Kempfe (“fighter”).
column3: noun. An ongoing winner in a game or contest.

column2: From Middle English charmynge; equivalent to charm + -ing.
column3: adjective. Pleasant, charismatic.

column2: From Middle English chereful, cherful, equivalent to cheer + -ful.
column3: adjective. Noticeably happy and optimistic.

column2: From New Latin chēmicus + -al.
column3: adjective. Of or relating to chemistry.

column2: The noun is a contraction of chest(en) (“(obsolete) chestnut tree; fruit of this tree, chestnut”) + nut. Chesten is a late variant of chesteine (obsolete), from Middle English chesten, chesteine, chasteine, chesteyne (“chestnut tree (Castanea sativa); fruit of this tree; wood of this tree”), from Old French chastaigne, chastaine (French châtaigne), from Latin castanea (“chestnut tree; fruit of this tree”) (whence Old English ċisten), from Ancient Greek κᾰστᾰ́νειᾰ (kăstắneiă), a variant of κᾰ́στᾰνᾰ (kắstănă, “sweet chestnut”); for further etymology, see that entry. Doublet of castanet. Noun sense 4 (“joke, phrase, etc., which has been repeated so often as to have grown ineffective or tiresome”) may refer to an 1816 play, The Broken Sword, by William Dimond (1781 – c. 1837), in which one character begins to relate a story in which a boy slips down from a cork tree, and another interrupts him to say that he had previously repeated the story many times, and always mentioned a chestnut tree. The adjective is probably from an attributive use of the noun; compare French (of hair) châtain (“chestnut”) (from châtaigne (“a chestnut”)) and marron (“brown”) (from marron (“a horse chestnut or chestnut”)).
column3: noun. An edible nut (technically a fruit) of the Spanish chestnut or sweet chestnut tree (Castanea sativa); also (chiefly preceded by a descriptive word), a nut from a related shrub or tree; or a similar nut from an unrelated plant.

column2: From Middle English childisch, from Old English ċildisċ. By surface analysis, child + -ish.
column3: adjective. Immature in thought or behaviour.

column2: From Middle English children, alteration of earlier childre ("children"; > English dialectal childer), from Old English ċildru, ċildra (“children”), nominative and accusative plural of ċild (“child”), equivalent to child + -ren.
column3: noun. plural of child

column2: From Middle English circuler, circuleer, circulere, from Old French circulier (French circulaire), from Late Latin circularis, from Latin circulus, diminutive of circus (“ring”). By surface analysis, circle + -ar.
column3: adjective. Of or relating to a circle.

column2: From Middle English cyvylien, from Old French civilien. Equivalent to civil + -ian.
column3: noun. A person following the pursuits of civil life, especially one who is not an active member of the armed forces.

column2: Borrowed from French civiliser, corresponding to civil + -ize.
column3: verb. American and Oxford British standard spelling of civilise.

column2: From French classifier. By surface analysis, class + -ify.
column3: verb. to identify by or divide into classes; to categorize

column2: From clear + -est.
column3: adjective. superlative form of clear: most clear

column2: From clear + -ing.
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of clear

column2: From Middle English clymbyng, clymbynge; equivalent to climb + -ing.
column3: noun. The sport of climbing, ascending a wall or a rock or another object using available holds, generally with the safety of a rope and belayer.

column2: From clinic + -al.
column3: adjective. Dealing with the practical management of patients, in practice at the point of care; as contrasted with other health care venues (see clinical medicine for more explanation).

column2: By surface analysis, clip + -ing.
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of clip

column2: From Middle English clothing, clathing, from Old English *clāþung, from Proto-West Germanic *klaiþungu (“clothing”), equivalent to clothe + -ing. Cognate with Scots clathing, claithing (“clothing”), Saterland Frisian Klodenge (“clothing”), West Frisian klaaiïng (“clothing”), Dutch kleding (“clothing”), German Kleidung (“clothing”), Danish klædning (“clothing, dress, attire”), Swedish kläding, klädning (“clothing, dress”). Doublet of the dialectal English term cleading, from Middle English clething; compare also cladding.
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of clothe

column2: Shortened from cobbler’s awls, for balls (testicles or nonsense)
column3: noun. plural of cobbler

column2: From Middle French coherent, from Latin cohaērēns, from co- + haereō. By surface analysis, cohere + -ent.
column3: adjective. Unified; sticking together; making up a whole.

column2: From French coïncider, from Medieval Latin coincidere, from con- + incidere, from in- (“into, to”) + cadere (“to fall, fall down, drop”).
column3: verb. To occupy exactly the same space.

column2: From Latin collāpsus (past participle of collābor).
column3: verb. To break apart and fall down suddenly; to cave in.

column2: From Middle English commencen, comencen (also as contracted comsen, cumsen), from Anglo-Norman comencer, from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre, formed from Latin com- + initiō (whence English initiate).
column3: verb. To begin, start.

column2: Inherited from Middle English comunly; equivalent to common + -ly.
column3: adverb. As a rule; frequently; usually.

column2: Borrowed from French communal, from Late Latin commūnālis, from Latin commūnis. Doublet of cominal.
column3: adjective. Pertaining to a community or a commune.

column2: From Middle English compilour, from Anglo-Norman compilour, from Old French compileur, from Latin compīlātōrem, equivalent to compile + -er.
column3: noun. One who compiles.

column2: From Middle English complaynen, from Old French complaindre, from Medieval Latin complangere (“to bewail, complain”), from Latin com- (“together”) + plangere (“to strike, beat, as the breast in extreme grief, bewail”); see plain, plaint.
column3: verb. To express feelings of pain, dissatisfaction, or resentment.

column2: From Middle English compleet (“full, complete”), borrowed from Old French complet or Latin completus, past participle of compleō (“to fill up, to complete”) (whence also complement, compliment), from com- + pleō (“to fill, to fulfill”) (whence also deplete, replete, plenty), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“to fill”) (English full).
column3: verb. To finish; to make done; to reach the end.

column2: From compose + -er.
column3: noun. One who composes; an author. Especially, one who composes music.

column2: Possibly from Malay kampong, kampung (“group of buildings, village”), via Dutch or Portuguese, altered under the influence of Etymology 2. Doublet of kampung.
column3: noun. An enclosure within which workers, prisoners, or soldiers are confined.

column2: From Middle English compressen, from Old French compresser, from Late Latin compressare (“to press hard/together”), from Latin compressus, the past participle of comprimō (“to compress”), itself from com- (“together”) + premō (“press”).
column3: verb. To make smaller; to press or squeeze together, or to make something occupy a smaller space or volume.

column2: From Middle English comprisen, from Old French compris, past participle of comprendre, from Latin comprehendere, contr. comprendere, past participle comprehensus (“to comprehend”); see comprehend. Compare apprise, reprise, surprise.
column3: verb. To be made up of; to consist of (especially a comprehensive list of parts).

column2: From compute + -er. Doublet of cantore, counter, and kontor. The sense referring to people first appears c. 1613 in the works of the poet Richard Brathwait. The sense referring to a machine first appears c. 1897 in the magazine Engineering.
column3: noun. A programmable electronic device that performs mathematical calculations and logical operations, especially one that can process, store and retrieve large amounts of data very quickly; now especially, a small one for personal or home use employed for manipulating text or graphics, accessing the Internet, or playing games or media.

column2: From Middle English conceyven, from Old French concevoir, conceveir, from Latin concipiō, concipere (“to devise, to conceive”).
column3: verb. To have a child; to become pregnant (with).

column2: Borrowed from Italian concerto, deverbal from concertare. Doublet of concert.
column3: noun. A piece of music for one or more solo instruments and orchestra.

column2: From Middle English concluden, borrowed from Latin conclūdere (“to shut up, close, end”).
column3: verb. To end; to come to an end.

column2: Borrowed from Latin concrētus, past participle of concrescō (to curdle) from con- (with, together) + crescō (to grow, rise).
column3: adjective. Real, actual, tangible.

column2: Borrowed from Middle French condenser, from Latin condēnsō.
column3: verb. To concentrate toward the essence by making more close, compact, or dense, thereby decreasing size or volume.

column2: From Latin cōnflīctus, from com- + flīctus, past participle of conflīgō (“to strike together”), from com- + flīgō (“strike”) (whence con-).
column3: noun. A clash or disagreement, often violent, between two or more opposing groups or individuals.

column2: From Middle French confronter, borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre, from con- + frontem (“front, forehead”).
column3: verb. To stand or meet facing, especially in competition, hostility or defiance; to come face to face with.

column2: Originally from Middle English confused (“frustrated, ruined”), from Anglo-Norman confus + Middle English -ed (past participial suffix), from Latin cōnfūsus, past participle of cōnfundō; now equivalent to confuse (a back-formation) + -ed.
column3: verb. simple past and past participle of confuse

column2: From Middle English consideren, from Middle French considerer, from Latin considerare.
column3: verb. To think about seriously.

column2: From Middle English constant, from Old French constant, from Latin constantem, accusative of constans, from cōnstāre (“to stand firm”). Displaced native Old English singal.
column3: adjective. Unchanged through time or space; permanent.

column2: From consume + -er.
column3: noun. One who, or that which, consumes.

column2: From Latin contemptus (“scorn”), from contemnō (“to scorn, despise”), from com- + temnō (“to despise”). Displaced native Old English forsewennes.
column3: noun. The state or act of contemning; the feeling or attitude of regarding someone or something as inferior, base, or worthless; scorn, disdain.

column2: From Middle English continuen, from Old French continuer, from Latin continuāre. Displaced native Middle English thurghwonen, from Old English þurhwunian.
column3: verb. To proceed with; to prolong.

column2: From Middle English, from Old French contract, from Latin contractus (noun), from contrahere (“to bring together, to bring about, to conclude a bargain”) [from con- (“with, together”) + trahere (“to draw, to pull”)] + -tus (suffix forming nouns from verbs).
column3: noun. An agreement between two or more parties, to perform a specific job or work order, often temporary or of fixed duration and usually governed by a written agreement.

column2: From Middle English contrarie, compare French contraire, from Old French contraire, from Latin contrārius (“opposite, opposed, contrary”), from contrā (“against”).
column3: adjective. Opposite; in an opposite direction; in opposition; adverse.

column2: From French contraster, from Latin contrāstāre (“to resist", "to withstand”), from contrā (“against”) + stō, stāre (“to stand”).
column3: noun. A difference in lightness, brightness or hue between two colours that makes them more or less distinguishable. The degree of this difference.

column2: From Middle English contreve (“to invent”), from Old French controver (Modern French controuver), from trover (“to find”) (French trouver).
column3: verb. To invent by an exercise of ingeniosity; to devise

column2: From Old French converser, from Latin conversor (“live, have dealings with”).
column3: verb. To talk; to engage in conversation.

column2: Borrowed from Latin convincō (“to refute, prove”), from con- + vincō (“to conquer, vanquish”). Doublet of convict. Displaced native Old English oferreċċan.
column3: verb. To make someone believe, or feel sure about something, especially by using logic, argument or evidence.

column2: Borrowed from French corridor, from Italian corridore (“long passage”) (= corridoio), from correre (“to run”).
column3: noun. A narrow hall or passage with rooms leading off it, as in a building or in a railway carriage.

column2: From Middle English couplynge; equivalent to couple + -ing.
column3: noun. The act of joining together to form a couple.

column2: From Middle English curteisie, curtesie, from Anglo-Norman curtesie, from Old French curteisie, cortoisie. Equivalent to courteous + -y (abstract noun suffix). By surface analysis, court + -esy.
column3: noun. Polite behavior.

column2: From cover + -age. First attested in 1912. Compare Middle English coverage (“a charge for having or stall or booth at a fair”).
column3: noun. An amount by which something or someone is covered.

column2: Present participle or participial adjective from cover (verb) + -ing; or, from Middle English coverynge, participle form of coveren, keveren (“to cover”).
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of cover

column2: Inherited from Middle English crakynge.
column3: noun. The thermal decomposition of a substance, especially that of crude petroleum in order to produce petrol / gasoline.

column2: Inherited from Middle English creacion, from Old French creacion (modern French création), from Latin creātiō, creātiōnis. By surface analysis, create + -ion. Displaced native Old English ġesċeaft.
column3: noun. Something created such as an invention or artwork.

column2: Borrowed from Late Latin creativus, from Latin creō. Equivalent to create + -ive. Displaced native Old English orþanclīċ.
column3: adjective. Tending to create things, or having the ability to create; often, excellently, in a novel fashion, or any or all of these.

column2: Inherited from Middle English creature (“a created thing”), borrowed via Old French creature, from Late Latin creātūra, from creō. By surface analysis, create + -ure. Displaced native Old English ġesċeaft. Doublet of craythur and critter.
column3: noun. A living being, such as an animal, monster, or alien.

column2: From Middle English credible, borrowed from Middle French credible, from Latin crēdibilis (“worthy of belief”), from crēdō (“believe”); see credit.
column3: adjective. Believable or plausible.

column2: From Middle English cryminal, borrowed from Anglo-Norman criminal, from Late Latin criminalis, from Latin crimen (“crime”).
column3: adjective. Against the law; forbidden by law.

column2: The plural form of criterion, formed according to the Ancient Greek -ον (-on) → -α (-a) pluralisation pattern.
column3: noun. plural of criterion

column2: From Latin criticus + English -al.
column3: adjective. Inclined to find fault or criticize.

column2: By surface analysis, cross + -ing.
column3: noun. Cross-breeding.

column2: By surface analysis, cruise + -ing.
column3: noun. Sailing about without an exact destination, especially for pleasure.

column2: By surface analysis, crush + -ing.
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of crush

column2: From culture + -al.
column3: adjective. Pertaining to culture.

column2: Inherited from Middle English cuppeborde, cupbord. Equivalent to cup + board. Phonetic variants show that the /p/ in the original forms had assimilated to the present-day /b/ by the 16th century; the etymological spelling has, however, dominated from the 18th century.
column3: noun. A board or table used to openly hold and display silver plate and other dishware; a sideboard; a buffet.

column2: Borrowed from Medieval Latin currentia. By surface analysis, current + -cy.
column3: noun. Money or other items used to facilitate transactions.

column2: From Middle English custumer, from Old French coustumier, costumier (compare modern French coutumier), from Medieval Latin custumarius (“a toll-gatherer, tax-collector”, noun), from custumarius (“pertaining to custom or customs”, adjective), from custuma (“custom, tax”). More at custom. By surface analysis, custom + -er.
column3: noun. A habitual patron, regular purchaser, returning client; a person or company who has a custom of buying from a particular business.

column2: From Middle French chilindre, cylindre, from Latin cylindrus, from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros), from κυλίνδω (kulíndō) "I roll or wallow" (intransitive). Doublet of calander and calender.
column3: noun. A surface created by projecting a closed two-dimensional curve along an axis intersecting the plane of the curve.

column2: From damage + -ing.
column3: adjective. Causing damage; harmful, injurious.

column2: From Middle English derknesse, from Old English deorcnes; equivalent to dark + -ness.
column3: noun. The state of being dark; lack of light; the absolute or comparative absence of light.

column2: From data + base.
column3: noun. A collection of (usually) organized information in a regular structure, usually but not necessarily in a machine-readable format accessible by a computer.

column2: From Middle English doghter, doughter, from Old English dohtor (“daughter”), from Proto-West Germanic *dohter, from Proto-Germanic *duhtēr, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰugh₂tḗr.
column3: noun. One’s female offspring.

column2: From Middle English daye-lighte, dey liȝht, dailiȝt, day-liht, dai-liht (also as days lyȝt, daies liht), equivalent to day + light. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Deegeslucht, Daisljoacht (“daylight”), West Frisian deiljocht (“daylight”), Dutch daglicht (“daylight”), German Tageslicht (“daylight”).
column3: noun. The natural light that is ambient in daytime, being mostly sunlight (both direct and indirect, on either sunny days or cloudy days).

column2: According to the Oxford English Dictionary, early usage refers to lines that do not move, such as one used in angling. Slightly later American usage refers to a boundary in a prison which prisoners must not cross. There is only indirect evidence that the sense of "due date" may be connected with this use of the term in prison camps during the American Civil War, when it referred to a physical line or boundary beyond which prisoners were shot. In 1904, in a report from the US Department of Commerce and Labor, the term is used for "minimum work goals" (and in contrast to bonus line): for example, as a typographer the line could be 18,000 ems per day; should one not cross this line, then that could have negative consequences. In 1917, the term is attested as a printing term for a guideline on the bed of a printing press beyond which text will not print. Three years later, the term is found in print in the sense of "time limit" in the closely connected publishing industry, indicating the time after which material would not make it into a newspaper or periodical.
column3: noun. A time limit in the form of a date on or before which something must be completed.

column2: From debug + -er.
column3: noun. A computer program that helps the user to test and debug other programs, by enabling their step-by-step execution controlled by the user, setting of breakpoints, and monitoring values of variables.

column2: Derived from Middle French, from Latin dēcīsiō, dēcīsiōnis, from dēcīdō (“to decide”).
column3: noun. The act of deciding.

column2: From Middle English decresen, alteration of discresen, from Anglo-Norman, Old French descreistre (French: décroître), from Latin decrescere.
column3: verb. Of a quantity, to become smaller.

column2: From Middle English dedicaten (“to dedicate”), from dedicat(e) (“dedicated”, also used as the past participle of dedicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), from Latin dēdicātus, the perfect passive participle of dēdicō (“to dedicate, proclaim”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
column3: verb. To set apart for a deity or for religious purposes; consecrate.

column2: From defeat + -ed.
column3: adjective. Subjugated, beaten, overcome.

column2: From defend + -ed.
column3: adjective. Having defenses.

column2: From Latin dēfīnītus, past participle of dēfīniō, whence also English define.
column3: adjective. Having distinct limits.

column2: degrade + -ed. See degrade and compare French degré (“step”).
column3: adjective. Feeling or having undergone degradation; deprived of dignity or self-respect.

column2: From Latin dēlētiōnem (“destruction, effacement”), from the past-participle stem of dēlēre (“to blot out, destroy, efface”). Equivalent to delete + -ion.
column3: noun. An item that has been or will be deleted.

column2: From Middle English delicat, from Latin dēlicātus (“giving pleasure, delightful, soft, luxurious, delicate, (in Medieval Latin also) fine, slender”), from dēlicia + -ātus (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), usually in plural dēliciae (“pleasure, delight, luxury”), from dēliciō (“to allure, entice”), from dē- (“away”) + laciō (“to lure, to deceive”), from Proto-Italic *lakjō (“to draw, pull”), of unknown ultimate origin. Compare delight, delicious and Spanish delgado (“thin, skinny”). The noun is from a substantivization of the adjective (see -ate).
column3: adjective. Easily damaged or requiring careful handling.

column2: From Middle English deliveri et al., from Anglo-Norman, from Old French delivrer.
column3: noun. The act of conveying something.

column2: From Latin dēlūsiō.
column3: noun. An adamant belief in a falsehood despite incontestable evidence.

column2: Past participle of dement + -ed, from Latin dēmentāre.
column3: adjective. Insane; mentally ill.

column2: Attested since the 16th century; from Middle French demoliss-, the stem of some conjugated forms of the verb demolir (“to destroy”, “to tear down”), from Latin dēmōlior (“to tear down”). Displaced native Old English tōweorpan (literally “to throw apart”).
column3: verb. To destroy (buildings, etc.), especially in a planned or intentional fashion.

column2: Borrowed from French dérangé.
column3: adjective. Disturbed or upset, especially mentally.

column2: From Middle English descriven, from Old French descrivre, from Latin dēscrībō (“to copy off, transcribe, sketch off, describe in painting or writing”), from dē (“off”) + scrībō (“write”); see scribe and shrive. Displaced native Old English āmearcian.
column3: verb. To represent in words.

column2: From design + -er.
column3: noun. A person who designs something, or who designs things as a profession.

column2: Borrowed from Latin dētēctor. Equals detect + -or (agent noun forming suffix).
column3: noun. A device capable of registering a specific substance or physical phenomenon, and that optionally sounds an alarm or triggers a warning.

column2: From Middle French diagonal, from Latin diagōnālis, from Ancient Greek διαγώνιος (diagṓnios, “from angle to angle”), from διά (diá, “across”) + γωνία (gōnía, “angle”).
column3: adjective. Joining two nonadjacent vertices (of a polygon or polyhedron).

column2: Inherited from Middle English dialog, from Old French dialoge (French dialogue), from Late Latin dialogus, from Ancient Greek διάλογος (diálogos, “conversation, discourse”), from διά (diá, “through, inter”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, discourse”), from διαλέγομαι (dialégomai, “to converse”), from διά (diá) + λέγειν (légein, “to speak”), equivalent to dia- (“between”) + -logue. Also analyzable as di- (“two”) + -alogue.
column3: noun. A conversation or other form of discourse between two or more individuals.

column2: From Old French diametre (French diamètre), from Latin diametros, from Ancient Greek διάμετρος (diámetros) (γραμμή (grammḗ)) (diametros grammē, “line measuring across”), from διά (diá, “across”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”). By surface analysis, dia- + -meter.
column3: noun. Any straight line between two points on the circumference of a circle that passes through the center of the circle; a chord that passes through the center of the circle.

column2: From Latin dictātor (“a chief magistrate”), from dictō (“dictate, prescribe”), from dīcō (“say, speak”). By surface analysis, dictate + -or, literally “one who dictates”. Compare Old English tictator (“absolute ruler of the Roman Republic”).
column3: noun. An authoritarian leader of a country, nation, or government.

column2: From direct + -ly.
column3: adverb. In a direct manner; in a straight line or course.

column2: Borrowed from Middle French directeur and its source Late Latin dīrēctōrem, from Latin dīrēctus. By surface analysis, direct + -or.
column3: noun. One who directs; the person in charge of managing a department or directorate (e.g., director of engineering), project, or production (as in a show or film, e.g., film director).

column2: From disable + -ed.
column3: adjective. Made incapable of use or action.

column2: From Middle English disagre (“to refuse to assent to”), from Anglo-Norman disagreer, disagrer, desagreer (“to refuse assent”), from Old French desagreer, desagrëer (“to be disagreeable; to be unpleasant”) (modern French désagréer (“to displease”)); the English word is analysable as dis- + agree.
column3: verb. To fail to agree; to have a different opinion or belief.

column2: From Middle French desastre, from Italian disastro, from dis- + astro (“star”), from Latin astrum (“star”), from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr.
column3: noun. An unexpected natural or man-made catastrophe of substantial extent causing significant physical damage or destruction, loss of life or sometimes permanent change to the natural environment.

column2: Alteration of French descompte, décompte, from Old French disconter, desconter (“reckon off, account back, discount”), from Medieval Latin discomputō (“to deduct, discount”), from Latin dis- (“away”) + computō (“to reckon, count”). By surface analysis, dis- + count.
column3: verb. To sell at a reduced price.

column2: From Middle English discoveren, from Old French descovrir, from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperiō, discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō. Displaced native Old English onfindan.
column3: verb. To find or learn something for the first time.

column2: From Old French discret, from Latin discrētus, past participle of discernō (“divide”), from dis- + cernō (“sift”). Doublet of discreet.
column3: adjective. Separate; distinct; individual; non- continuous.

column2: From Middle English disgisen, disguisen, borrowed from Old French desguiser (modern French déguiser), itself derived from des- (“dis-”) (from Latin dis-) + guise (“guise”) (from a Germanic source).
column3: noun. Material (such as clothing, makeup, a wig) used to alter one’s visual appearance in order to hide one's identity or assume another.

column2: Borrowed from Middle French desordre (modern French désordre), from Old French desordre, from des- + ordre; by surface analysis, dis- + order (<< Latin ōrdō). Compare typologically Russian непоря́док (neporjádok), беспоря́док (besporjádok), неуря́дица (neurjádica) (akin to ряд (rjad), поря́док (porjádok)).
column3: noun. Absence of order; state of not being arranged in an orderly manner.

column2: From dispose + -al.
column3: noun. A disposition; an arrangement, categorization, or classification of things.

column2: From Middle English distance, distaunce, destance (“disagreement, dispute; discrimination; armed conflict; hostility; trouble; space between two points; time interval”), from Anglo-Norman distance, distaunce, destance, Middle French distance, and Old French destance, destaunce, distaunce (“debate; difference, distinction; discord, quarrel; dispute; space between two points; time interval”) (modern French distance), and directly from their etymon Latin distantia (“difference, diversity; distance, remoteness; space between two points”) (whence also Late Latin distantia (“disagreement; discrepancy; gap, opening; time interval”)), from distāns (“being distant; standing apart”) + -ia (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns). Distāns is the present active participle of distō (“to be distant; to stand apart; to differ”), from dis- (prefix meaning ‘apart, asunder; in two’) + stō (“to stand”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand (up)”)). The verb is derived from the noun.
column3: noun. An amount of space between points (often geographical points), usually (but not necessarily) measured along a straight line.

column2: From Middle English distincte, past participle of distincten (“to distinguish, discern”), from Old French destincter, from Latin distinctus, past participle of distinguere (“to distinguish”); see distinguish.
column3: adjective. Capable of being perceived very clearly.

column2: Borrowed from Latin distractus, from distrahō (“to pull apart”), from dis- + trahō (“to pull”).
column3: verb. To divert the attention of.

column2: The verb is from Middle English distressen, from Old French destrecier (“to restrain, constrain, put in straits, afflict, distress”); compare French détresse. Ultimately from Medieval Latin as if *districtiō, an assumed frequentative form of Latin distringō (“to pull asunder, stretch out”), from dis- (“apart”) + stringō (“to draw tight, strain”). The noun is from Middle English distresse, from Old French destrece, ultimately also from Latin distringō.
column3: noun. Physical or emotional discomfort, suffering, or alarm, particularly of a more acute nature.

column2: From French district, from Medieval Latin districtus (“a district within which the lord may distrain, also jurisdiction”), from Latin districtus, past participle of distringere (“to draw asunder, compel, distrain”), from dis- (“apart”) + stringere (“to draw tight, strain”). Doublet of Detroit.
column3: noun. An administrative division of an area.

column2: From Middle English divisioun, from Old French division, from Latin dīvīsiō, dīvīsiōnem, noun of process form from perfect passive participle dīvīsus (“divided”), from dīvidō (“divide”). Doublet of divisio.
column3: noun. The act or process of dividing anything.

column2: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin doctrina (“teaching, instruction, learning, knowledge”), from doctor (“a teacher”), from docere (“to teach”); see doctor.
column3: noun. A belief or tenet, especially about philosophical or theological matters.

column2: Borrowed from Middle French document, from Latin documentum.
column3: noun. An original or official paper used as the basis, proof, or support of anything else, including any writing, book, or other instrument conveying information pertinent to such proof or support.

column2: From Middle French domestique, from Latin domesticus, from domus (“house, home”).
column3: adjective. Of or relating to the home.

column2: Borrowed from Middle French dominant.
column3: noun. The fifth major tone of a musical scale (five major steps above the note in question); thus G is the dominant of C, A of D, and so on.

column2: Borrowed from Latin dominātus, perfect active participle of dominor (“to rule, have dominion”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dominus (“lord, master”) + -or (verb-forming suffix).
column3: verb. To govern, rule or control by superior authority or power.

column2: From Middle English donacion, donation, from Middle French donation, from Latin dōnātiō (“a present”), from dōnō (“to give”), from dōnum (“a gift”). Recorded in English since the 15th century. Equivalent to donate + -ion.
column3: noun. A voluntary gift or contribution for a specific cause.

column2: From Middle English doutfull, douteful, equivalent to doubt + -ful.
column3: adjective. Subject to, or causing doubt.

column2: From down- + hill.
column3: adverb. Down a slope.

column2: From drag + -ing.
column3: adjective. That drags.

column2: Learned borrowing from Latin drāmaticus. By surface analysis, drama + -tic.
column3: adjective. Of or relating to the drama.

column2: From draw + back. Compare setback.
column3: noun. A disadvantage; something that detracts or takes away.

column2: From Middle English dredful, dredfull, dredeful (also dreful). By surface analysis, dread + -ful.
column3: adjective. Full of something causing dread, whether Genuinely horrific, awful, or alarming; dangerous, risky. Unpleasant, awful, very bad (also used as an intensifier). Awesome, awe-inspiring, causing feelings of reverence.

column2: From Middle English dressing, dressinge, dressynge, equivalent to dress + -ing.
column3: noun. Material applied to a wound for protection or therapy.

column2: Inherited from Middle English [Term?]. By surface analysis, drink + -ing.
column3: noun. An act or session by which drink is consumed, especially alcoholic beverages.

column2: By surface analysis, drop + -ing.
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of drop

column2: From Middle English duracioun, from late Old French duracion, from Medieval Latin dūrātiō.
column3: noun. An amount of time or a particular time interval.

column2: From dynamic + -ics.
column3: noun. The branch of mechanics that is concerned with the effects of forces on the motion of objects.

column2: The noun is derived from Middle English economike, iconomique (“household management”), and then: from οἰκονόμος (oikonómos, “master of a house; household manager, steward; administrator, manager”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, suffix meaning ‘of or relating to’ forming adjectives). Οἰκονόμος (Oikonómos) is derived from οἶκος (oîkos, “dwelling place, house; estate”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ- (“(verb) to enter in; to settle; (noun) settlement”)) + νόμος (nómos, “law, ordinance”) (from νέμω (némō, “to distribute; to possess”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to distribute; to give; to take”)) + -ος (-os, suffix forming o-grade action nouns from verbs)). Noun sense 2.2 (“one who manages the income of a vacant benefice”) is from Italian economo, from Late Latin oeconomus (“housekeeper, steward; administrator, especially of a religious foundation”), from Ancient Greek οἰκονόμος (oikonómos, “master of a house; household manager, steward; administrator, manager”): see above. The adjective is derived from the noun; compare the adjective senses in Middle and Old French, Latin, and Ancient Greek. By surface analysis, economy + -ic.
column3: adjective. Pertaining to an economy.

column2: From educate + -ed.
column3: adjective. Having attained a level of higher education, such as a college degree.

column2: From Middle English eightetene, eiȝtene, ehtetene, from Old English eahtatīene, eahtatēne, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutehun. Cognate with West Frisian achttjin, Dutch achttien, German achtzehn, Danish atten. Equivalent to eight + -teen.
column3: numeral. The cardinal number occurring after seventeen and before nineteen, represented in Roman numerals as XVIII and in Arabic numerals as 18.

column2: From Middle English eleccioun, eleccion, from Anglo-Norman eleccioun, from Latin ēlectiōn-, stem of ēlectiō (“choice, selection”), from ēligō (“to pluck out, to choose”). Equivalent to elect + -ion. Displaced native Old English cyre (“choice, free will, election”).
column3: noun. A process of choosing a leader, members of parliament, councillors, or other representatives by popular vote.

column2: First attested in c. 1646 in a publication by Thomas Browne. From New Latin ēlectricus (“electrical; of amber”), from ēlectr(um) (“amber”) + -icus (“adjectival suffix”); from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron, “amber”); related to ἠλέκτωρ (ēléktōr, “shining sun”), of unknown origin (see which for more). The Latin term was apparently used first with the sense electrical in 1600 by the English physician and scientist William Gilbert in his work De Magnete.
column3: adjective. Of, relating to, produced by, operated with, or utilising electricity; electrical.

column2: Blend of electric + ion, coined by Anglo-Irish scientist George Stoney in 1891, changed by him multiple times from an earlier electrolion and original electrine (used as early as 1874) as the name for the electric charge associated with a univalent ion. Compare electro-, -on. The particle ("corpuscule") was discovered in 1896. The name electrion was proposed for the particle in 1906 but curtailed because Hendrik Lorentz preferred electron.
column3: noun. The subatomic particle having a negative charge and orbiting the nucleus; the flow of electrons in a conductor constitutes electricity.

column2: From Middle English elefant, elefaunt, from Old French elefant, elefan, olifant, re-latinized in Middle French as elephant, from Latin elephantus, from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās) (gen. ἐλέφαντος (eléphantos)). Believed to be derived from an Afroasiatic form such as Proto-Berber *eḷu (“elephant”) (compare Tamahaq êlu, Tamasheq alu) or Egyptian ꜣbw (“elephant; ivory”). More at ivory. Replaced Middle English olifant (from the aforementioned Old French form, from Vulgar Latin *olifantus), which replaced Old English elpend (“elephant”).
column3: noun. A large mammal of the family Elephantidae in the order Proboscidea, having a trunk, and native to Africa and Asia.

column2: From elevate + -or.
column3: noun. Anything that raises or uplifts.

column2: From Middle French eligible, from Latin eligibilis, from ēligō (“to select, to choose”).
column3: adjective. Allowed to and meeting the necessary conditions required to participate in or be chosen for something.

column2: From embed + -ed.
column3: adjective. Part of; firmly, or securely surrounded; lodged solidly into; deep-rooted.

column2: By surface analysis, emerge + -ing.
column3: adjective. Becoming prominent; emergent; rising.

column2: From Latin emphasis, from Ancient Greek ἔμφασις (émphasis, “significance”), from ἐμφαίνω (emphaínō, “to present; to indicate”), from ἐν- (en-, “in”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to show”).
column3: noun. Special weight or forcefulness given to something considered important.

column2: From employ + -ee. First attested in the early 19th century, possibly modeled after French employé.
column3: noun. A person who provides labor to a company or another person.

column2: From employ + -er, first attested in the late 16th century. Compare French employeur.
column3: noun. A person, firm or other entity which pays for or hires the services of another person.

column2: The verb is from Middle English endeveren (“to make an effort”); the noun is from Middle English endevour, from the verb. Endeveren is from (putten) in dever (“(to put oneself) in duty”), from in + dever (“duty”), partially translating Middle French (se mettre) en devoir (de faire) (“(to make it) one's duty (to do), to endeavour (to do)”) (from Old French devoir, deveir (“duty”)).
column3: noun. A sincere attempt; a determined or assiduous effort towards a specific goal; assiduous or persistent activity.

column2: The noun is derived from: The verb is derived from the noun.
column3: noun. A soldier engaged in designing or constructing military works for attack or defence, or other engineering works. A soldier in charge of operating a weapon; an artilleryman, a gunner.

column2: From enhance + -ed.
column3: adjective. In a version or form that has been improved or made better than some other standard form.

column2: From Latin ēnormis. An assimilated form of ex- (“out of”) + norma (“rule, norm”) + -ous.
column3: adjective. Deviating from the norm; unusual, extraordinary.

column2: From Middle English entyerly, entierly, enterely, entyreliche, equivalent to entire + -ly.
column3: adverb. To the full or entire extent.

column2: From Middle English enterete, from Old French entiereté, from Latin integritās, from integer (“complete, whole”). Doublet of integrity.
column3: noun. The whole; the complete or amount.

column2: From Middle French entrance (“entry”). Replaced native Middle English ingang (“entrance, admission”), from Old English ingang (“ingress, entry, entrance”).
column3: noun. The action of entering, or going in.

column2: From French enveloppe. The engineering sense is derived from flight envelope. The verb is from the noun.
column3: noun. A paper or cardboard wrapper used to enclose small, flat items, especially letters, for mailing.

column2: From French envisager, from en (“in”) + visage (“visage”); equivalent to en- + visage.
column3: verb. To conceive or see something within one's mind; to imagine or envision.

column2: Borrowed from Middle French equalité (modern French égalité), from Latin aequālitās, aequālitātem. Doublet of equity. By surface analysis, equal + -ity
column3: noun. The fact of being equal.

column2: From Old French, from Latin aequātiō (“an equalizing”). Morphologically equate + -ion
column3: noun. The act or process of equating two or more things, or the state of those things being equal (that is, identical).

column2: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐσωτερικός (esōterikós, “belonging to an inner circle”), from ἐσωτέρω (esōtérō, “further inside”), comparative of ἔσω (ésō, “within”), from ἐς (es), εἰς (eis, “into”) (the term esoteric referred originally to the secret teachings of Greek philosophers, versus public or exoteric ones).
column3: adjective. Intended for or likely to be understood by only a small number of people with a specialized knowledge or interest, or an enlightened inner circle.

column2: From Middle English estimat, borrowed from Latin aestimātus (“valuing, estimate”, only used in the ablative singular: "aestimātū..." (in valuing...)), from aestimō + -tus (“action noun-forming suffix”).
column3: noun. A rough calculation or assessment of the value, size, or cost of something.

column2: From Middle English eternyte, from Old French eternité, from Latin aeternitās. Displaced native Old English ēcnes.
column3: noun. Existence without end, infinite time.

column2: Back-formation from evaluation.
column3: verb. To draw conclusions from examining; to assess; to appraise.

column2: From evening + -s (adverbial suffix). Compare with Dutch avonds, Low German avends, German abends.
column3: adverb. In the evening, during the evening.

column2: From event + -ual; compare French éventuel. The third sense is influenced by any of several European languages, including German eventuell, French éventuel, Italian eventuale, Spanish eventual, Swedish eventuell.
column3: adjective. Finally resulting or occurring (after a period of time); inevitable.

column2: From Middle English everidayes, every daies, every dayes (“everyday, daily, continual, constant”, adjective, literally “every day's”), equivalent to every + day.
column3: adjective. Appropriate for ordinary use, rather than for special occasions.

column2: An alteration of earlier everychone after every, from Middle English everichon. By surface analysis, every + one.
column3: pronoun. Every person.

column2: From Middle English evidence, from Old French [Term?], from Latin evidentia (“clearness, in Late Latin a proof”), from evidens (“clear, evident”); see evident.
column3: noun. Facts or observations presented in support of an assertion.

column2: From examine + -er.
column3: noun. A person who investigates someone or something.

column2: From Middle English eschaunge, borrowed from Anglo-Norman eschaunge, from Old French eschange (whence modern French échange), from the verb eschanger, from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre (from Latin ex with Late Latin cambiō). Spelling later changed on the basis of ex-, with pronunciation following. By surface analysis, ex- + change.
column3: noun. An act of exchanging or trading.

column2: From Middle English exercise, from Old French exercise, from Latin exercitium. Displaced native Old English plega (“an exercise”) whence Modern English play.
column3: noun. Any activity designed to develop or hone a skill or ability.

column2: Borrowed from French explicite, from Latin explicitus (“disentangled, easy”), variant of explicātus.
column3: adjective. Very specific, clear, or detailed.

column2: From expos(e) + -ure.
column3: noun. The condition of being exposed, uncovered, or unprotected.

column2: From Late Middle English, from Medieval Latin externus (“outward, external”), from exter / exterus (“on the outside, outward”).
column3: adjective. Outside of something; on the exterior.

column2: From Middle English eiȝesiht, ieȝesihte, ehsihthe, eihsihthe, eȝhesihthe, equivalent to eye + sight.
column3: noun. Vision or the faculty of sight.

column2: From Middle English facilite, from Middle French facilité, and its source, Latin facilitās. By surface analysis, facile + -ity. Doublet of faculty.
column3: noun. The physical means or contrivances to make something (especially a public service) possible; the required equipment, infrastructure, location etc.

column2: From Middle English fairness, fæȝernesse, from Old English fæġernes (“fairness; beauty; pleasantness”), equivalent to fair + -ness. Cognate with Old High German fagarnessi (“fairness”).
column3: noun. The property of being fair or equitable.

column2: From Middle English feithful, equivalent to faith + -ful.
column3: adjective. Loyal; adhering firmly to person or cause.

column2: From Middle English familiar, familier, from Latin familiāris (“pertaining to servants; pertaining to the household”). By surface analysis, family + -ar. Piecewise doublet of familial. Displaced native Old English hīwcūþ.
column3: adjective. Known to one, or generally known; commonplace.

column2: From Middle English farewel, from fare wel ! (and the variants with the personal pronoun " fare ye well " and " fare you well " used in the Renaissance), an imperative expression, possibly further derived from Old English * far wel !, equivalent to fare (“to fare, travel, journey”) + well. Compare Scots farewele, fairweill (“farewell”), Saterland Frisian Foarwäil (“farewell”), West Frisian farwol (“farewell”), German Fahrwol, Fahrwohl, East Frisian forwal, Dutch vaarwel (“farewell (sadly)”), Danish farvel (“farewell”), Norwegian farvel (“farewell”), Swedish farväl (“farewell”), Faroese farvæl (“goodbye”), Icelandic far vel (“farewell”). The extensive list of cognates suggests a postulated ultimate Proto-Germanic phrase of origin, possibly something akin to *far wela.
column3: noun. A wish of happiness or safety at parting, especially a permanent departure.

column2: From Anglo-Norman fesable, from Latin facere, Old French fesable, faisable (“doable”), from fere, faire (“to do”) + -able.
column3: adjective. Able to be done in practice.

column2: From feature + -ed.
column3: adjective. displayed with special treatment

column2: From feed + back.
column3: noun. Critical assessment of a process or activity or of their results.

column2: First attested in 1852. Ultimately from Latin fēminīnus, from fēmina (“woman”). See also feminine, feminism.
column3: adjective. Relating to or in accordance with feminism.

column2: From Middle English festival (adjective), from Old French festival (“festive”), from Late Latin fēstīvālis, from Latin fēstīvus (“festive”). By surface analysis, festive + -al. Displaced native Old English frēols. The noun is shortened from festival day, from Middle English festival dai, festiuall day (“feast day, festival”).
column3: adjective. Pertaining to a feast or feast day; festive.

column2: From Middle English feghtyng, fyȝtynge, fightand, feghtand, feghtande, feightand, feȝtand, viȝtinde, feihtende, from Old English feohtende, from Proto-Germanic *fehtandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *fehtaną (“to comb, struggle, contend with”), equivalent to fight + -ing.
column3: adjective. Engaged in war or other conflict.

column2: From filter + -ed.
column3: adjective. With a filter (e.g., a cigarette).

column2: From final + -ize.
column3: verb. To make final or firm; to finish or complete.

column2: From fire + work. Compare Saterland Frisian Fjuurwierk (“firework”), West Frisian fjoerwurk (“firework”), Dutch vuurwerk (“firework”), Low German Füürwark, Füerwark (“firework”), German Feuerwerk (“firework”), Danish fyrværkeri (“firework”), Swedish fyrverkeri (“firework”), Faroese fýrverk (“firework”).
column3: noun. A device using gunpowder and other chemicals which, when lit, emits a combination of coloured flames, sparks, whistles or bangs, and sometimes made to rocket high into the sky before exploding, used for entertainment or celebration.

column2: From flash + -ing.
column3: noun. A sudden blazing or bursting, as of fire or water.

column2: From Middle French flexible, from Latin flexibilis, from flectō (“to bend, curve”). Morphologically flex + -ible.
column3: adjective. Capable of being flexed or bent without breaking; able to be turned or twisted without breaking.

column2: By surface analysis, float + -ing.
column3: adjective. That floats or float.

column2: From Middle English flusshyng, flusshynge, equivalent to flush + -ing.
column3: noun. The act by which something is flushed.

column2: From Middle English folwer, folwere, folewer, from Old English folgere (“follower; attendant; disciple”), equivalent to follow + -er. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Foulger, West Frisian folger, Dutch volger, German Folger, Swedish följare.
column3: noun. One who follows, comes after another.

column2: From Middle English fotbal, footbal, equivalent to foot + ball, because the ball was primarily manipulated with the feet in early versions of the game (though some modern varieties involve more handling than kicking). The name for the briefcase is a play on “dropkick”, the code name of an early version of the nuclear war plan.
column3: noun. A sport played on foot in which teams attempt to get a ball into a goal or zone defended by the other team.

column2: From foot + note.
column3: noun. A short piece of text, often numbered, placed at the bottom of a printed page, that adds a comment, citation, reference etc, to a designated part of the main text.

column2: From Middle English forceably, equivalent to forcible + -ly.
column3: adverb. In a forcible manner, by force, against one's will.

column2: From Middle English forecasten, forcasten, equivalent to fore- + cast. The noun is from Middle English forecast, forcast.
column3: verb. To estimate how something will be in the future.

column2: Morphologically forgive + -n.
column3: verb. past participle of forgive

column2: From formal + -ly.
column3: adverb. In a formal manner.

column2: From former + -ly.
column3: adverb. at some time in the past

column2: From forward + -s (adverbial suffix).
column3: adverb. Synonym of forward in most senses.

column2: From Middle English [Term?]; from Old French fontaine (whence modern fontaine); from Late Latin fontana, from Latin fontanus, fontaneus, adjectives from fons (“source, spring”).
column3: noun. A natural source of water; a spring.

column2: From Middle English fourtene, from Old English fēowertīene, from Proto-Germanic *fedurtehun. Cognate with West Frisian fjirtjin, Dutch veertien, German vierzehn, Danish fjorten. Equivalent to four + -teen.
column3: numeral. The cardinal number occurring after thirteen and before fifteen.

column2: From Middle English fraccioun (“a breaking”), from Anglo-Norman, Old French fraccion, from Medieval Latin fractio (“a fragment, portion”), from earlier Latin fractio (“a breaking, a breaking into pieces”), from fractus, past participle of frangere (“to break”) (whence English frangible), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- (English break). Doublet of frazione.
column3: noun. A part of a whole, especially a comparatively small part.

column2: From Late Middle English fragment, from Latin fragmentum (“a fragment, remnant”), from frangō (“to break”) + -mentum.
column3: noun. A part broken off; a small, detached portion; an imperfect part, either physically or not.

column2: By surface analysis, freeze + -ing.
column3: adjective. Suffering or causing frost.

column2: From Old French frequent, from Latin frequens (“crowded, crammed, frequent, repeated, etc.”), possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *bʰrekʷ- (“to cram together”).
column3: adjective. Done or occurring often; common.

column2: From Middle French friction and directly from Latin frictionem, nom. frictio (“a rubbing, rubbing down”).
column3: noun. The rubbing of one object or surface against another.

column2: From Middle English frendly, freendly, frendely, frendlich, from Old English frēondlīċ, from Proto-Germanic *frijōndlīkaz, equivalent to friend + -ly. Cognate with Saterland Frisian früntelk, fjuntelk (“friendly”), West Frisian freonlik (“friendly”), Dutch vriendelijk (“friendly”), German Low German fründelk, frünnelk (“friendly”), German freundlich (“friendly”). Doublet of friendlike.
column3: adjective. Generally warm, approachable and easy to relate with in character.

column2: From Middle English *frightenen, equivalent to fright + -en.
column3: verb. To cause to feel fear; to scare; to cause to feel alarm or fright.

column2: From Middle French function, from Old French fonction, from Latin functiō (“performance, execution”), from functus, perfect participle of fungor (“to perform, execute, discharge”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg- (“to enjoy”).
column3: noun. What something does or is used for.

column2: Borrowed from Ancient Greek γαλακτικός (galaktikós, “milky”), from γάλα (gála, “milk”). Doublet of galactico.
column3: adjective. Relating to a galaxy. Relating to the Milky Way galaxy.

column2: From garble + -ing.
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of garble

column2: From gas + -ol (suffix used in the names of oils) + -ine (suffix used in the names of derivatives). So called because it was originally used in the manufacture and enrichment of domestic gases, such as air gas. Some sources suggest that the name originated from the brand name Cazeline, a petroleum -derived lighting oil, from the surname of the man who first marketed it in 1862, John Cassell, and the suffix –eline, from Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “oil, olive oil”), from ἐλαία (elaía, “olive”). Gasolene is found from 1863, and gasoline from 1864.
column3: noun. A flammable liquid consisting of a mixture of refined petroleum hydrocarbons, mainly used as a motor fuel; petrol.

column2: From Latin generō (“beget, procreate, produce”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from genus (“a kind, race, family”, gener- in compounds) + -ō; see genus. Compare Italian generare, French générer (and its older (and now obsolete) English cognate from Middle French, gender (“engender, breed, copulate”)).
column3: verb. To bring into being; give rise to.

column2: From Middle French genereux, and its source, Latin generōsus (“of noble birth”), from genus (“race, stock”).
column3: adjective. Noble in behaviour or actions; principled, not petty; kind, magnanimous.
