column2: From Ancient Greek γένεσις (génesis, “origin”). Coined by English biologist William Bateson in 1905 in a letter to zoologist Adam Sedgwick, and first used publicly by Bateson at a lecture to the International Conference on Plant Hybridization in 1906.
column3: noun. The branch of biology that deals with the transmission and variation of inherited characteristics, in particular chromosomes and DNA.

column2: From Middle English gemetry, geometrie, from Old French geometrie (modern French géométrie), from Latin geōmetria, from Ancient Greek γεωμετρία (geōmetría, “geometry, land-survey”), from γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs, “geometer, land measurer”), from γῆ (gê, “earth, land, country”) + -μετρία (-metría, “measurement”), from μέτρον (métron, “a measure”). By surface analysis, geometer + -y or geo- + -metry. Doublet of gematria. Displaced native Old English eorþcræft, literally, " earth - craft ".
column3: noun. The branch of mathematics dealing with spatial relationships.

column2: From global + -ly.
column3: adverb. In all places or situations.

column2: From Middle English glorious, from Anglo-Norman glorius and Old French glorïos, from Latin glōriōsus. Displaced native Middle English wulderful, from Old English wuldorfull (“glorious”), among other terms. Equivalent to glory + -ous.
column3: adjective. Exhibiting attributes, qualities, or acts that are worthy of or receive glory.

column2: From gold + fish.
column3: noun. A type of small fish, Carassius auratus, typically orange -colored.

column2: From Middle English goodnesse, godnesse, from Old English gōdnes (“goodness; virtue; kindness”), from Proto-West Germanic *gōdnassī (“goodness”), equivalent to good + -ness. Cognate with Scots guidness (“goodness”), West Frisian goedens (“goodness”), Old High German guotnessī (“goodness”), Middle High German guotnisse (“goodness”), Russian годность (godnostʹ, “suitability, fitness”).
column3: noun. The state or characteristic of being good.

column2: From Middle English gorgeouse, a borrowing from Middle French gorgias (“elegant, fashionable”), from Old French gourgias, gorgias (“gorgeous, gaudy, flaunting, gallant, fine”), of uncertain origin, but apparently connected with Old French gorgias (“a gorget, ruffle for the neck”), from Old French gorge (“bosom, throat”). See gorge. Semantic evolution probably akin to "swelling of the throat or bosom due to pride, bridling up" to "assume an air of importance, flaunting".
column3: adjective. Sumptuously dressed.

column2: From Middle English governour, from Old French gouvreneur, from Latin gubernator, from Ancient Greek κυβερνήτης (kubernḗtēs, “steersman, pilot, guide”), from κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, to drive, to guide, to act as a pilot”), of disputed origin. By surface analysis, govern + -or. Doublet of gubernator.
column3: noun. The chief executive officer of a first - level administrative division of a country.

column2: From Middle English graduat(e) (“(noun) a graduate of a university; (adjective) graduate, having graduated”, also used as the past participle of graduaten (“to graduate”)), borrowed from Medieval Latin graduātus (“graduated, graduate”), perfect passive participle of graduō (“to graduate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from gradus (“step”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). The noun is originally derived within Latin from the adjective via substantivization, see -ate (noun-forming suffix). Sense 10 of the verb, relating to Japanese entertainment, is a semantic loan from Japanese 卒業 (sotsugyō).
column3: noun. A person who is recognized as having completed any of various levels of education.

column2: Borrowed from Italian graffiti, from graffito, from graffire, borrowed from Ancient Greek γρᾰ́φω (grắphō, “to write”), from Proto-Hellenic *grə́pʰō, from Proto-Indo-European *gerbʰ-.
column3: noun. Drawings or words drawn on a surface in a public place, usually made without authorization.

column2: Borrowed from Italian graffito.
column3: noun. An informal inscription, as by a worker or vandal.

column2: From grate (“(obsolete) serving to gratify, agreeable, pleasing; grateful, thankful”) + -ful (suffix forming adjectives with the sense of tending to have or thoroughly having a quality). Grate is a learned borrowing from Latin grātus (“agreeable, pleasing; beloved, dear; grateful, thankful”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“to express approval, praise; to elevate”).
column3: adjective. Of a person or their actions, feelings, etc.: expressing gratitude or appreciation; appreciative, thankful.

column2: Inherited from Middle English gryndynge. By surface analysis, grind + -ing.
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of grind

column2: From Middle English gessyng, gessynge, equivalent to guess + -ing.
column3: noun. The act of making a guess; estimate or prediction; foresight.

column2: From guide + -ance. Displaced native Old English lādtēowdōm.
column3: noun. The act or process of guiding.

column2: Origin uncertain. Either from gull (“to dupe, trick, fool”) + -ible; or alternatively from Middle English gole, goll, gol (“an unfledged bird, silly fellow”), perhaps from Old Norse gulr (“yellow, pale”), from the hue of its down.
column3: adjective. Easily deceived or duped; naive, easily cheated or fooled.

column2: From Middle English handbok, from Old English handbōc (“handbook”), possibly reinforced as a calque of German Handbuch (“handbook”). By surface analysis, hand + book. Compare West Frisian hânboek (“handbook”), Dutch handboek (“handbook”), German Low German Handbook (“handbook”), Danish håndbog (“handbook”), Swedish handbok (“handbook”), Icelandic handbók (“handbook”).
column3: noun. A topically organized book of reference on a certain field of knowledge, regardless of size, but archetypally one to be kept readily at hand.

column2: From hand-in-cap, in reference to holding the game stakes in a cap.
column3: noun. Something that prevents, hampers, or hinders.

column2: From Middle English handlinge, hondlunge, from Old English handlung (“handling”), equivalent to handle + -ing. Cognate with Dutch handeling (“trade, operation, action”), German Handlung (“act, action”), Swedish handling (“act, deed, action”).
column3: noun. A touching, controlling, managing, using, taking care of, etc., with the hand or hands, or as with the hands.

column2: American English; hang + over. First sense was first attested in 1904. Third sense was first attested in 1894.
column3: noun. Negative effects, such as headache or nausea, caused by previous drunkenness due to (excessive) consumption of alcohol.

column2: From hard + back, formed in analogy to earlier paperback.
column3: noun. A book with a solid binding.

column2: From Middle English hardshipe, equivalent to hard + -ship.
column3: noun. Difficulty or trouble; hard times.

column2: From Middle English hardware; equivalent to hard + -ware; attested since the mid-15th century.
column3: noun. Fixtures, equipment, fasteners, tools, and devices used for general-purpose construction and repair of a structure or object. Also such equipment as sold as stock by a store of the same name, e.g. hardware store.

column2: From Middle English harmles, from Old English *hearmlēas, from Proto-Germanic *harmalausaz (“without harm; harmless”), equivalent to harm + -less. Cognate with German harmlos (“harmless”), Danish harmløs (“harlmess”), Swedish harmlös (“harmless”).
column3: adjective. Incapable of causing harm or danger; safe.

column2: From Middle English hevedeche, from Old English hēafodeċe. By surface analysis, head + ache.
column3: noun. A pain or ache in the head.

column2: From head + line.
column3: noun. The heading or title of a magazine or newspaper article.

column2: From Middle English hertely, herteliche, heorteliche, from Old English ġeheortlīċe (“whole-heartedly, vigorously”), equivalent to hearty + -ly.
column3: adverb. In a hearty manner.

column2: From Middle English helples, from Old English *helplēas (“helpless”) from Proto-Germanic *helpōlausaz, equivalent to help + -less. Compare Dutch hulpeloos (“helpless”), German hilflos (“helpless”), Danish hjælpeløs (“helpless”) and Swedish hjälplös (“helpless”).
column3: adjective. Unable to defend oneself.

column2: From Middle English heritage, from Old French eritage, heritage (modern French héritage), ultimately derived (through suffixation) from Latin hērēs. By surface analysis, herit + -age.
column3: noun. An inheritance; property that may be inherited.

column2: Borrowed from Latin haesitātus, perfect passive participle of haesitō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), intensive of haereō (“to hesitate, stick fast; to hang or hold fast”). Displaced native Old English wandian. Compare French hésiter.
column3: verb. To stop or pause respecting decision or action; to be in suspense or uncertainty as to a determination.

column2: From Latin historicus (“historical”), from Ancient Greek ἱστορικός (historikós, “exact; historical”). Cognate with French historique. By surface analysis, history + -ic.
column3: adjective. Very important; noteworthy: having importance or significance in history.

column2: The adverb is derived from Middle English hiderto (“to the present time, until now; up to this point”), from hider (“in this direction, to or toward this place; up to the present time, until now”) (from Old English hider (“to here, hither”)) + to (“in the direction of, toward; etc.”). By surface analysis, hither + to. The adjective is derived from the adverb.
column3: adverb. Up to this or that time.

column2: From Middle English honestly, honestlyche, honestliche, equivalent to honest + -ly.
column3: adverb. In an honest manner.

column2: From honor + -ary, modelled after French honoraire, from Latin honōrārius.
column3: adjective. Given as an honor, with no duties attached, and without payment.

column2: From hope + -less. Compare Swedish hopplös.
column3: adjective. Without hope; despairing; not expecting anything positive.

column2: First attested in Middle English (alternately as horrible and orrible) in 1303: from Old French horrible, orrible, orible, from Latin horribilis, from horr(ēre) (“tremble”) + -ibilis (“-ible”).
column3: noun. A thing that causes horror; a terrifying thing, particularly a prospective bad consequence asserted as likely to result from an act.

column2: From Middle English horribly, horribely, horribliche, horriblelyche, equivalent to horrible + -ly.
column3: adverb. In a horrible way; very badly.

column2: Borrowed from Latin horrificus, from horreō (“to be afraid”) + -ficō (“to make”).
column3: adjective. Causing horror; horrifying.

column2: From Middle English hospital, hospitall, from Old French hospital (Modern French hôpital), from Late Latin hospitālis, hospitāle (“hospice, shelter, guesthouse”), from noun use of Latin hospitālis (“hospitable”), from hospes (“host, guest”). Doublet of hotel and hostel. Displaced native Middle English lechehous, from Old English lǣċehūs (literally “doctor house”).
column3: noun. A large medical facility, usually in a building with multiple floors, where seriously ill or injured patients are given extensive medical or surgical treatment.

column2: Inherited from Middle English humanyte, humanite, humanitye, from Old French humanité, from Latin hūmānitās. By surface analysis, human or humane + -ity. Partly displaced mankind, from Old English mancynn (literally “human race”).
column3: noun. Humankind; human beings as a group.

column2: From Middle English humorous (compare Medieval Latin hūmorōsus), equivalent to humor + -ous.
column3: adjective. Full of humor or arousing laughter; funny.

column2: Borrowed from French hydrogène (“hydrogen”), coined by the French chemists Louis-Bernard Guyton de Morveau (1737–1816) and Antoine Lavoisier (1743–1794) from hydro- (prefix meaning ‘water’) + -gène (suffix denoting a producer of something), from the fact that water is produced as a compound when hydrogen is oxidized. By surface analysis, hydro- (prefix meaning ‘water’) + -gen (suffix denoting a producer of something).
column3: noun. The lightest chemical element (symbol H), with an atomic number of 1 and atomic weight of 1.008.

column2: From French identifier, from Medieval Latin identicus + Latin faciō.
column3: verb. To establish the identity of someone or something.

column2: From Middle English ydemptite, from Middle French identité and its etymon Late Latin idemptitās, identitās, from idem (“the same”) + -tās (suffix forming abstract nouns) as a calque of Ancient Greek ταὐτότης (tautótēs, “sameness”).
column3: noun. Sameness, identicalness; the quality or fact of (several specified things) being the same.

column2: Borrowed from French idéologie, from idéo- + -logie (equivalent to English ideo- + -logy). Cognate with, but not derived from, idea. Coined 1796 by Antoine Destutt de Tracy. Modern sense of “doctrine” attributed to use of related idéologue (“ideologue”) by Napoleon Bonaparte as a term of abuse towards political opponents in early 1800s.
column3: noun. Doctrine, philosophy, body of beliefs or principles belonging to an individual or group.

column2: From Old French ignorant, from Latin ignōrāns (“unaware, unknowing”). By surface analysis, ignore + -ant.
column3: adjective. Unknowledgeable or uneducated; characterized by ignorance.

column2: From Old French illusion, from Latin illūsiō, from illūdere, from in- (“at, upon”) + lūdere (“to play, mock, trick”). Displaced native Old English dwimmer.
column3: noun. A distortion of sensory perception where real stimuli lead to a false or misleading impression of reality.

column2: Learned borrowing from Latin imāginēs.
column3: noun. plural of imago

column2: From Middle French immature. Partially displaced unripe, from Old English unrīpe (“unripe, immature”).
column3: adjective. Occurring before the proper time; untimely, premature (especially of death).

column2: From the present participle of Latin imminēre (“to overhang”), from mineō ("to project, overhang"), related to minae (English menace) and mons (English mount). Compare with eminent.
column3: adjective. About to happen, occur, or take place very soon, especially of something which won't last long.

column2: From Latin immortālis, from prefix im- (“not”) (from in-) + mortālis (“mortal”) (from mors (“death”), combining form mort- + adjectival suffix -alis), equivalent to im- + mortal. Displaced native undeadly, from Old English undēadlīċ. The term referring to the Persian soldiers was a Calque of Ancient Greek ἀθάνατος (athánatos). One suggestion claimed that "Immortals" were named by the ancient Greeks because wounded soldiers were quickly replaced, while another claimed that it was because Greek informants confused Old Persian *anauša- (“immortal, without death”) with Old Persian *anūšiya- (“companion, royal bodyguard”).
column3: adjective. Not susceptible to death; living forever; never dying.

column2: From Middle English imperial, from Old French imperial, from Latin imperiālis (“of the empire or emperor, imperial”), from imperium (“empire, imperial government”) + -ālis, from imperō (“command, order”), from im- (“form of in”) + parō (“prepare, arrange; intend”). Displaced Old English cāserlīċ.
column3: adjective. Related to an empire, emperor, or empress.

column2: From Middle French implicite, from Latin implicitus, past participle of implico (“to infold, involve, entangle”); see implicate.
column3: adjective. Suggested indirectly, without being directly expressed; Implied.

column2: Inherited from Middle English imprisonen, emprisounen, emprisonen, from Old French emprisonner. Equivalent to im- + prison.
column3: verb. To put in or as if in prison; confine somebody against their will.

column2: Recorded since 1412, from Middle French incident, from Latin incidens, the present active participle of incidō (“to happen, befall”), itself from in- (“on”) + -cidō, the combining form of cadō (“to fall”).
column3: noun. An event or occurrence.

column2: From incline + -ed.
column3: adjective. At an angle to the horizontal; slanted or sloped.

column2: From in (adverb) + coming (adjective).
column3: adjective. Coming (or about to come) in; arriving.

column2: From Middle English encresen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman encreistre, from Latin increscere (“to increase”), from in (“in, on”) + crescō (“grow”). The noun is from Middle English encres, from the verb.
column3: verb. (of a quantity, etc.) To become larger or greater, to greaten.

column2: Borrowed from Latin indicātus, perfect passive participle of indicō (“to point out, indicate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in, to”) + dicō (“to declare, (originally) to point”). See also diction and index.
column3: verb. To point out; to discover; to direct to a knowledge of; to show; to make known.

column2: From Middle French indirect, from Late Latin indirectus (“not direct”).
column3: adjective. Not direct: Not of obvious or immediate cause, but as a secondary result.

column2: From Middle English industry, industrie, from Old French industrie, from Latin industria (“diligence, activity, industry”), from industrius (“diligent, active, zealous”), from Old Latin indostruus (“diligent, active”); origin unknown. Perhaps from indu (“in”) + ūst-, ūstr-, stem of ūrō (“burn, burn up, consume”, verb), related to Old High German ūstrī (“industry”), Old English andūstrian (“to hate, detest”, literally “to be consumed with zeal”).
column3: noun. The tendency to work persistently.

column2: From Middle English enfamouse, in-fames, infamous, from Medieval Latin īnfāmōsus, from Latin īnfāmis; by surface analysis, in- + famous. Displaced native Old English unhlīsful.
column3: adjective. Having a bad reputation; disreputable; notorious; unpleasant or evil; widely known, especially for something scornful.

column2: Borrowed from Latin īnferior (“lower in situation or place”), comparative of īnferus (“below, underneath”).
column3: adjective. Lower in rank, status, or quality.

column2: From Middle English infinite, from Old French infinit and its etymon Latin īnfīnītus, from in- (“not”) + fīnis (“end”) + the perfect passive participle ending -ītus. By surface analysis, in- + finite. Doublet of infinito. Displaced native Old English unġeendodlīċ.
column3: adjective. Indefinably large, countlessly great; immense.

column2: From Middle English infinite, from Old French infinité, from Latin īnfīnitās (“unlimitedness”), from negative prefix in- (“not”), + fīnis (“end”), + noun of state suffix -tās. By surface analysis, infinite + -ity.
column3: noun. Endlessness, unlimitedness, absence of a beginning, end or limits to size.

column2: From in- + formal.
column3: adjective. Not formal or ceremonious.

column2: From inform + -ed.
column3: verb. simple past and past participle of inform

column2: From Latin inhaerentem, accusative singular of inhaerēns, present active participle of inhaereō (“to be closely connected with; to adhere to”).
column3: adjective. Naturally as part or consequence of something.

column2: Borrowed from Latin initiātus, perfect passive participle of initiō (“to begin, originate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from initium (“a beginning”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), from initus (“an entrance, coming in, approach”) + -ium, from ineō + -tus, from in- + eō (“to go”). Cognate with French initier.
column3: verb. To begin; to start.

column2: From Middle English innocent, from Old French innocent, inocent, borrowed from Latin innocēns (“harmless, inoffensive”), from in- (“not”) + nocēns, present participle of noceō (“to hurt”). By surface analysis, in- (“not”) + nocent (“harmful; guilty”). Displaced native Old English unsċyldiġ.
column3: adjective. Free from guilt, sin, or immorality.

column2: From in- + secure, or from Medieval Latin insēcūrus, itself from in- (“in-, un-, non-”) + sēcūrus (“safe, certain”). Piecewise doublet of unsecure and unsure.
column3: adjective. Not secure.

column2: Borrowed from Middle French instance, from Latin īnstantia (“a being near, presence, also perseverance, earnestness, importunity, urgency”), from īnstāns (“urgent”); see instant.
column3: noun. Urgency of manner or words; an urgent request; insistence.

column2: From Latin īnstīnctus, past participle of īnstinguō (“to incite, to instigate”), from in (“in, on”) + stinguō (“to prick”).
column3: noun. A natural or inherent impulse or behaviour.

column2: From Latin īnstrūctus, perfect passive participle of īnstruō (“I instruct; I arrange, furnish, or provide”).
column3: verb. To teach by giving instructions.

column2: Borrowed from Middle French integral, from Medieval Latin integrālis, from Latin integer (“entire”); see integer.
column3: adjective. Constituting a whole together with other parts or factors; not omittable or removable.

column2: From inter- + act.
column3: verb. To act upon each other. To engage in communication and other shared activities (with someone).

column2: From Middle English interest, from Old French interesse and interest (French intérêt), from Medieval Latin interesse, from Latin interesse.
column3: noun. The price paid for obtaining, or price received for providing, money or goods in a credit transaction, calculated as a fraction of the amount or value of what was borrowed.

column2: From Latin interior (“inner, interior”).
column3: adjective. Within any limits, enclosure, or substance; inside; internal; inner.

column2: From Middle English internall, internalle, borrowing from New Latin internālis (“of or pertaining to the inner part”), from internus (“inward, internal”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, intern + -al.
column3: adjective. Of or situated on the inside.

column2: From Middle English interval, intervalle, from Old French intervalle, entreval, from Latin intervallum (“space between, interval, distance, interval of time, pause, difference; literally, space between two palisades or walls”), from inter (“between”) + vallum (“palisade, wall”).
column3: noun. A distance in space.

column2: Borrowed from Latin intimātus, the perfect passive participle of intimō (“to put or bring into, to impress, to make familiar”) (see -ate (adjective forming suffix)), from intimus (“inmost, innermost, most intimate”), superlative of intus (“within”), from in (“in”); see interior.
column3: adjective. Closely acquainted; familiar.

column2: From Middle French invasion, from Late Latin invāsiōnem, accusative of invāsiō.
column3: noun. A military action consisting of a large armed force of one geopolitical entity entering territory controlled by another such entity, generally with the objective of conquering territory or altering the established government.

column2: Borrowed from Latin inventor. By surface analysis, invent + -or.
column3: noun. One who invents, either as a hobby or as an occupation.

column2: From involve + -ed.
column3: adjective. Complicated.

column2: Borrowed from Latin irrītātus, perfect passive participle of irrītō (“excite, irritate, incite, stimulate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
column3: verb. To provoke impatience, anger, or displeasure in.

column2: A rendering into English of French isolé.
column3: adjective. Placed or standing apart or alone; in isolation.

column2: From Middle English juggement, borrowed from Old French jugement, from Late Latin iūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdicō. Partially displaced doom. By surface analysis, judge + -ment.
column3: noun. The act of judging.

column2: From Latin iūnctiō (“union, joining, uniting”), from iungō (“join, attach together”). Equivalent to join + -tion.
column3: noun. The act of joining, or the state of being joined.

column2: Borrowed from Latin iuvenīlis (“youthful; juvenile”), from iuvenis (“young; a youth”) + -īlis (suffix forming adjectives indicating a relationship or a pertaining to). Iuvenis is ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁en- (“young”), from *h₂óyu (“long life; lifetime”) (from *h₂ey- (“age; life”)) + *h₁én (“in”).
column3: adjective. Young; not fully developed.

column2: From key + board.
column3: noun. A set of keys laid out in a gridlike pattern, used for typing on a typewriter, computer, etc.

column2: From Middle English kyndenesse, equivalent to kind + -ness.
column3: noun. The state of being kind.

column2: From Middle English londlord, landlorde, from Old English landhlāford, equivalent to land + lord. Cognate with Scots landlaird, Middle Low German lantlord (“homeowner, landlord”).
column3: noun. A person that leases real property; a lessor.

column2: From Middle English langage, language, from Old French language, from Vulgar Latin *linguāticum, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech, language”), from Old Latin dingua (“tongue”), from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s (“tongue, speech, language”). Doublet of langaj. Displaced native Old English ġeþēode.
column3: noun. A body of words, and set of methods of combining them (called a grammar), understood by a community and used as a form of communication.

column2: From Middle English laughynge; equivalent to laugh + -ing.
column3: noun. verbal noun of laugh: the action of the verb to laugh.

column2: From Middle English laughter, laghter, laȝter, from Old English hleahtor (“laughter, jubilation, derision”), from Proto-Germanic *hlahtraz (“laughter”), from Proto-Indo-European *klek-, *kleg- (“to shout”). Cognate with German Gelächter (“laughter, hilarity, merriment”), Danish and Norwegian latter (“laughter”), Icelandic hlátur (“laughter”). More at laugh.
column3: noun. The sound of laughing, produced by air so expelled; any similar sound.

column2: From Middle English lavatorie, from Late Latin lavātōrium, from Latin lavāre (“to wash”) + -ium (forming places related to an activity). As a place to pan gold, via Spanish lavadero. Doublet of lavatorium and laver. See also lave.
column3: noun. A vessel or fixture for washing, particularly: A laver: a washbasin. A bathtub. A piscina: the basin used for washing communion vessels. A lavabo: the basin used for washing one 's hands before handling the Eucharist. A baptismal font: the basin used for baptism, used figuratively for the washing away of sins. A plumbing fixture used for washing: a sink.

column2: From lazy + -ness.
column3: noun. The quality of being lazy

column2: From Middle English lernyng, lernynge, from Old English leornung (“learning, study”), from Proto-West Germanic *liʀnungu (“learning”), equivalent to learn + -ing. Cognate with Old Saxon lernunga, German Lernung.
column3: noun. An act in which something is learned.

column2: From lecture + -er.
column3: noun. A person who gives lectures, especially as a profession.

column2: From Middle English lyftyme, equivalent to life + time. Cognate with Icelandic líftími (“lifetime”). Compare also Saterland Frisian Lieuwendstied, Dutch leeftijd and levenstijd, German Low German Levenstied, German Lebenszeit, Danish livstid, Swedish livstid.
column3: noun. The duration of the life of someone or something.

column2: From light + -ing.
column3: noun. The equipment used to provide illumination; the illumination so provided.

column2: From Middle English lykewise, lykewyse, lyke wyse, lijk wise, a shortened form of Middle English in lik wise (“in like wise”); equivalent to like + -wise. Compare with otherwise.
column3: adverb. In a similar manner.

column2: From listen + -er.
column3: noun. Someone who listens, especially to a speech or a broadcast.

column2: From French littéraire.
column3: adjective. Relating to literature.

column2: Inherited from Middle English litterate, borrowed from Latin lītterātus, līterātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix). Doublet of literato and literatus. Displaced native Old English stæfwīs.
column3: adjective. Able to read and write; having literacy.

column2: Borrowed from Latin locatio, locationis (“a placing”), from locare (“to place, put, set, let”), from locus (“a place”). Equivalent to locate + -ion.
column3: noun. A particular point or place in physical space.

column2: From Middle English loupe (“opening in a wall”) + hole, from a Germanic source. By surface analysis, loop + hole. Compare Medieval Latin loupa, lobia and Middle Dutch lupen (“to watch”).
column3: noun. A slit in a castle wall; today, any similar window for shooting a ranged weapon or letting in light.

column2: c. 1600, "descend, sink, grow less or lower" (intransitive), from lower (adj.), comparative of low (adj.). Transitive meaning "let down, cause to descend" attested from 1650s. Related: Lowered; lowering. In the transitive sense "to cause to descend" the older verb was low. From Middle English lahghenn, (c. 1200), which continued in use into the 18c.
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of lower

column2: From Middle English magasyne, from Middle French magasin (“warehouse, store”), from Italian magazzino (“storehouse”), ultimately from Arabic مَخَازِن pl (maḵāzin), plural of مَخْزَن (maḵzan, “storeroom, storehouse”), noun of place from خَزَنَ (ḵazana, “to store, to stock, to lay up”). First attested in the 1580s.
column3: noun. A nonacademic, periodical publication which consists of articles by multiple writers on some broad topic or theme. A radio or television show where each episode comprises a variety of features or segments, akin to the format of a print magazine.

column2: From magnet + -ic.
column3: adjective. Of, relating to, operating by, or caused by magnetism.

column2: From Middle English mayntenen, from Old French maintenir, from Late Latin manūteneō, manūtenēre (“I support”), from Latin manū (“with/in/by the hand”, ablative of manus) + tenēre (“to hold”).
column3: verb. To keep up; to preserve; to uphold (a state, condition etc.).

column2: From Middle French maiorité, from Medieval Latin maiōritātem, accusative of Latin maiōritās, from Latin maior (“greater”). Morphologically major + -ity.
column3: noun. More than half (50%) of some group.

column2: From man- + saging
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of manage

column2: From man + power.
column3: noun. The total number of all available workers; the workforce.

column2: From manual + -ly.
column3: adverb. By hand.

column2: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin marginālis, equivalent to margin + -al.
column3: adjective. Of, relating to, or located at or near a margin or edge; also figurative usages of location and margin (edge).

column2: From Middle English mariage, from Old French mariage, from marier (“to marry”), from Latin marītō (“marry”, verb, literally “give in marriage”), from marītus (“lover”, “nuptial”), from mas (“male, masculine, of the male sex”). Equivalent to marry + -age. Doublet of maritage. Displaced native Old English sinsċipe.
column3: noun. The state of being married.

column2: From Middle English material, from Late Latin māteriālis, from Latin māteria (“wood, material, substance”), from māter (“mother”). Displaced native Middle English andweorc, andwork (“material, matter”) (from Old English andweorc (“matter, substance, material”)). Doublet of materiel.
column3: adjective. Of, relating to, or consisting of matter, especially physical.

column2: From Latin maximus + English -ize.
column3: verb. To make as large as possible.

column2: From Middle English menetime, equivalent to mean + time. Adverb is by ellipsis from in the meantime.
column3: noun. The time spent waiting for another event; time in between.

column2: From Middle English mekanyk (“mechanical”), from Old French mecanique, from Latin mechanicus (“of or belonging to machines or mechanics, inventive”), from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós, “pertaining to machines or contrivance, mechanic, ingenious, inventive”), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “a machine, contrivance”); see machine.
column3: adjective. mechanical; relating to mechanics or the laws of motion in physics

column2: From Middle English medicin, from Middle French medicine, from Old French medecine, from Latin medicīna (“the healing art, medicine, a physician's shop, a remedy, medicine”), feminine of medicīnus (“of or belonging to physic or surgery, or to a physician or surgeon”), from medicus (“a physician, surgeon”). The extended sense of "Indigenous magic" is a calque of Ojibwe mashkiki (“medicine”) or mide (or cognates in related languages) when used in compounds such as Grand Medicine Society, medicine lodge, medicine dance, medicine bag, medicine wheel, medicine man, Medicine Line, and bad medicine or place names such as Medicine Hat, Medicine Creek, etc. Displaced native Old English lybb (“drug, medicine”).
column3: noun. A substance which specifically promotes healing when ingested or consumed in some way; a pharmaceutical drug.

column2: From French médiéval (“medieval”), from Latin medium (“middle”) + aevum (“age”).
column3: adjective. Of or relating to the Middle Ages, the period from approximately 500 to 1500 AD.

column2: From mega- + byte.
column3: noun. One million (10, or 1,000,000) bytes or 1,000 kilobytes.

column2: From mental + -ly.
column3: adverb. In a mental manner; an idea thought out in one's mind, as opposed to an idea spoken orally.

column2: From Middle French métaphore, from Latin metaphora, from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá), from μεταφέρω (metaphérō, “to transfer, apply”), from μετά (metá, “with, across, after”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).
column3: noun. The use of a word, phrase, concept, or set of concepts to refer to something other than its literal meaning, invoking an implicit similarity between the thing described and what is denoted by the word, etc., that is used.

column2: From Middle English midnight, from Old English midniht, from Proto-Germanic *midjanahts (“midnight”), equivalent to mid- + night. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Midnoacht (“midnight”), Old High German mittinaht (“midnight”), Danish midnat (“midnight”), Swedish midnatt (“midnight”), Icelandic miðnætti (“midnight”). Compare also Saterland Frisian Middernoacht (“midnight”), Dutch middernacht (“midnight”), German Mitternacht (“midnight”).
column3: noun. The middle of the night: the sixth temporal hour, equidistant between sunset and sunrise.

column2: From Middle English militari, from Old French militaire, from Latin mīlitāris, from mīles (“soldier”) + -āris (whence -ary). Doublet of militaire.
column3: adjective. Characteristic of members of the armed forces.

column2: From Middle English myndles, myndelees, myndeles, mendlees, from Old English myndlēas, ġemyndlēas (“foolish, senseless”), equivalent to mind + -less.
column3: adjective. Showing a lack of forethought or sense.

column2: From Latin minimus + -ize.
column3: verb. To make (something) smaller or as small as possible; shrink; reduce.

column2: From Middle English ministre, from Old French ministre, from Latin minister (“an attendant, servant, assistant, a priest's assistant or other under official”), from minor (“less”) + -ter; see minor. Doublet of Minorite.
column3: noun. A person who is trained to preach, to perform religious ceremonies, and to afford pastoral care at a Protestant church.

column2: From Late Middle English minoritie, from Middle French minorité, and its source Late Latin minōritās, from Latin minor. Morphologically minor + -ity.
column3: noun. The state or condition of being smaller, inferior, or subordinate to something or someone else; lesserness.

column2: From mis- + guide.
column3: verb. To guide poorly or incorrectly; to lead astray or into error.

column2: From mis- + place.
column3: verb. To put something somewhere and then forget its location; to mislay.

column2: From mis- + print.
column3: noun. An accidental mistake in print.

column2: Morphologically mistake + -n.
column3: verb. past participle of mistake

column2: Borrowed from Late Latin mnemonicus or its etymon Ancient Greek μνημονῐκός (mnēmonĭkós, “pertaining to memory or remembrance, memorial”) + English -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Mνημονῐκός (Mnēmonĭkós) is derived from μνήμων (mnḗmōn, “mindful, remembering”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives); while μνήμων (mnḗmōn) is from μνάομαι (mnáomai, “to be mindful, remember”) (from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to mind; to think”)) + -μων (-mōn, suffix forming adjectives and agent nouns).
column3: adjective. Especially of a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.: intended to help in remembering.

column2: From model + -ing.
column3: noun. The art of sculpting models from clay etc. to create a representation of something.

column2: From Middle English moderat(e) (“moderate, temperate”), borrowed from Latin moderātus, perfect active participle of moderor (“to regulate, to restrain, to moderate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from moder-, modes-, a stem appearing also in modestus (“moderate, discreet, modest”), from modus (“a measure”); see mode and modest. Doublet of moderato. Displaced native Old English ġemetlīċ (“moderate”) and metegian (“to moderate”). Cognate with French modéré.
column3: adjective. Not excessive; acting in moderation.

column2: From modify + -ed.
column3: adjective. changed; altered

column2: Borrowed from French molécule, from New Latin molecula (“a molecule”), diminutive of Latin moles (“a mass”).
column3: noun. The smallest particle of a specific element or compound that retains the chemical properties of that element or compound; two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds.

column2: Borrowed from Latin mōmentum. Doublet of moment and movement.
column3: noun. Of a body in motion: the tendency of a body to maintain its inertial motion; the product of its mass and velocity, or the vector sum of the products of its masses and velocities.

column2: From Latin monopōlium, from Ancient Greek μονοπώλιον (monopṓlion, “a right of exclusive sale”), from μόνος (mónos, “sole”) + πωλέω (pōléō, “to barter, sell”). By surface analysis, mono- + -poly.
column3: noun. A situation, by legal privilege or other agreement, in which solely one party (company, cartel etc.) exclusively provides a particular product or service, dominating that market and generally exerting powerful control over it.

column2: From Anglo-Norman moralité, Middle French moralité, from Late Latin mōrālitās (“manner, characteristic, character”), from Latin mōrālis (“relating to manners or morals”), from mōs (“manner, custom”). equivalent to moral + -ity.
column3: noun. Recognition of the distinction between good and evil or between right and wrong; respect for and obedience to the rules of right conduct; the mental disposition or characteristic of behaving in a manner intended to produce morally good results.

column2: Inherited from Middle English moreover, moreovere, morover, mooreover, more-overe, mare over, equivalent to more + over.
column3: adverb. In addition to what has been said.

column2: From motive + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French motiver.
column3: verb. To provide someone with an incentive to do something; to encourage; to actuate.

column2: From motor + way.
column3: noun. A highway with grade-separated crossings (rather than level crossings) and designed (and only permitted) for high-speed motor- traffic (in Europe motor vehicles with a higher speed limit than 40 km/h) running in two directions on one separate carriageway each.

column2: From Middle English mountayne, mountain, montaigne, from Anglo-Norman muntaine, muntaigne, from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem (“mountain”), from Proto-Indo-European *monti (compare Welsh mynydd (“mountain”), Albanian mat (“bank, shore”), Avestan 𐬨𐬀𐬙𐬌 (mati, “promontory”)), from *men- (“to project, stick out”). Displaced native English barrow (from Old English beorg) and down (from Old English dūn), and partially displaced non-native Old English munt, from Latin mōns (whence English mount).
column3: noun. An elevation of land of considerable dimensions rising more or less abruptly, forming a conspicuous figure in the landscape, usually having a small extent of surface at its summit.

column2: From mount + -ing.
column3: adjective. That continues to mount; steadily rising or accumulating.

column2: From Middle English mevement, from Old French movement (modern French mouvement), from movoir + -ment; cf. also Medieval Latin movimentum, from Latin movere (“move”). Doublet of moment and momentum. In this sense, displaced native Old English styring, which led to Modern English stirring. Morphologically move + -ment.
column3: noun. Physical motion between points in space.

column2: From French multiple, itself from Late Latin multiplus.
column3: determiner. More than one (followed by plural).

column2: From Old French multiplier, from Latin multiplicō, from multi (“many”) + plicō (“to fold”). The noun presumably derives from the verb.
column3: verb. To increase the amount, degree or number of (something).

column2: From Middle English murderere; equivalent to murder + -er.
column3: noun. A person who commits murder.

column2: From Middle English musician, musicien, from Old French musicien (“musician”), equivalent to musike + - ien. By surface analysis, music + -ician.
column3: noun. A composer, conductor, or performer of music; specifically, a person who sings and/or plays a musical instrument as a hobby, occupation, or profession.

column2: From mutual + -ly.
column3: adverb. In the same way, each to the other; reciprocally.

column2: From Latin mȳthicus + -al; by surface analysis, myth + -ical.
column3: adjective. Existing in myth.

column2: From Middle English nameles, equivalent to name + -less. Cognate with Dutch naamloos (“nameless”), German namenlos (“nameless”), Danish navnløs (“nameless”), Swedish namnlös (“nameless”), Icelandic nafnlaus (“nameless, anonymous”).
column3: adjective. Not having a name.

column2: From Middle French national, corresponding to nation + -al.
column3: adjective. Pertaining to a nation or country, especially as a whole; affecting, shared by, or existing throughout all of a nation; the state.

column2: From Middle English needlees, nedelees, nedeles, equivalent to need + -less.
column3: adjective. Not needed; unnecessary.

column2: From Middle English negative, negatif, from Old French negatif, from Latin negātīvus (“that denies, negative”), from negāre (“to deny”); see negate.
column3: adjective. Not positive or neutral; bad; undesirable; unfavourable.

column2: From Middle English newe-comere, equivalent to new- + comer. Compare Old English nīwcumen (“new comer, neophyte, novice”).
column3: noun. One who has recently come to a community; a recent arrival.

column2: From Middle English neke name, alteration (due to a rebracketing of an ekename as a nekename) of earlier ekename (“nickname”), from eke (“additional”) + name. Compare Old Norse aukanafn, auknafn, auknefni, Faroese eyknevni, Danish øgenavn, Norwegian Nynorsk aukenamn, Swedish öknamn, and German Low German Ökelname. For other similar cases of incorrect division, see also apron, daffodil, newt, orange, umpire.
column3: noun. A familiar, invented name for a person or thing used instead of the actual name of the person or thing, often based on some noteworthy characteristic.

column2: The adjective is first attested in 1450, in Middle English, the verb in 1545; partly from Middle English nominat(e) (“named, designated”), from Latin nōminātus, perfect passive participle of nōminō (“to name”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), from nōmen (“a name”). Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.
column3: verb. To name someone as a candidate for a particular role or position, including that of an office.

column2: From non- (“no, none, lack of”) + sense, from c. 1610. Compare the semantically similar West Frisian ûnsin (“nonsense”), Dutch onzin (“nonsense”), German Unsinn (“nonsense”), English unsense (“nonsense”).
column3: noun. Letters or words, in writing or speech, that have no meaning or pattern or seem to have no meaning.

column2: From normal + -ly.
column3: adverb. Under normal conditions or circumstances; usually; most of the time

column2: From Middle English northerne, from Old English norþerne, from Proto-West Germanic *norþrōnī, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrōnijaz. Cognate with Old High German nordrōni and Old Norse norrœnn. Morphologically north + -ern.
column3: adjective. Of, facing, situated in, or related to the north; northerly.

column2: From Latin notātiō, equivalent to notate + -ion or note + -ation.
column3: noun. The act, process, method, or an instance of representing by a system or set of marks, signs, figures, or characters.

column2: From now + adays.
column3: adverb. At the present time; in the current era.

column2: From Middle English noysaunce, from Anglo-Norman nusaunce, nussance and Old French nuisance, from nuisir (“to harm”), from Latin nocēre. Doublet of nocence and nocency.
column3: noun. A minor annoyance or inconvenience.

column2: From Middle English numerous from Latin numerōsus (“numerous, abundant; harmonious”), from numerus (“number”). Doublet of numerose. Analyzeable as numero- + -ous.
column3: determiner. An indefinite large number of.

column2: From observe + -er.
column3: noun. One who makes observations, monitors or takes notice.

column2: Borrowed from Latin obsolētus (“worn out, gone out of use”), past participle of obsolēscere (“to wear out, fall into disuse, grow old, decay”); see obsolesce.
column3: adjective. No longer in use or no longer useful; now disused or neglected (often in favour of something newer, better, or more fashionable); outmoded.

column2: From Latin past participle stem obstruct- (“blocked up”), from verb obstruere, from ob (“against”) + struere (“pile up, build”).
column3: verb. To block or fill (a passage) with obstacles or an obstacle. block.

column2: From Middle English occasioun, from Middle French occasion, from Old French occasiun, from Latin occāsiōnem, noun of action from perfect passive participle occāsus, from verb occidō, from prefix ob- (“down", "away”) + verb cadō (“fall”).
column3: noun. A favorable opportunity; a convenient or timely chance.

column2: From Middle English offendour, offender, offendir, equivalent to offend + -er.
column3: noun. One who gives or causes offense, or does something wrong.

column2: From offer + -ing. Displaced native Old English hūsl.
column3: noun. gerund of offer The act by which something is offered. That which has been offered; a sacrifice.

column2: From Middle English official, from Old French official, from Latin officiālis, from Latin officium (“duty, service”), by surface analysis, office + -ial.
column3: adjective. Of or about an office or public trust.

column2: From Middle English omissioun, from Old French omission, from Late Latin omissio, omissionem, from Latin omitto.
column3: noun. The act of omitting.

column2: Borrowed from Latin operātor, from operor (“work, labour”). Equivalent to operate + -or.
column3: noun. A person or organisation that operates a device, system, service, etc.

column2: Borrowed from Latin oppōnēns (“opposing”), present active participle of oppōnō (“to oppose”).
column3: noun. One who opposes another; one who works or takes a position against someone or something; one who attempts to stop the progress of someone or something.

column2: Inherited from Middle English opposit, borrowed from Old French oposite, from Latin oppositus, perfect passive participle of oppōnō (“to oppose”). Compare oppose.
column3: adjective. Located directly across from something else, or from each other.

column2: Back-formation from optimist. First attested in 1844.
column3: verb. To act optimistically or as an optimist.

column2: From option + -al.
column3: adjective. Not compulsory; left to personal choice; elective.

column2: From Anglo-Norman ordenarie, ordenaire et al., Middle French ordinaire, and their source, Medieval Latin ordinarius, noun use of Latin ōrdinārius (“regular, orderly”), from ōrdō (“order”).
column3: noun. A person with authority; authority, ordinance. A person having immediate jurisdiction in a given case of ecclesiastical law, such as the bishop within a diocese. A courier; someone delivering mail or post. A judge with the authority to deal with cases himself or herself rather than by delegation. The chaplain of Newgate prison, who prepared condemned prisoners for death.

column2: From Middle English organizen, organysen, partly from Middle French organiser and partly from its etymon, Medieval Latin organizō, from Latin organum (“organ”). By surface analysis, organ + -ize.
column3: verb. To arrange in working order.

column2: From Middle English original, from Old French original, from Late Latin orīginālis (“primitive, original”), from Latin orīgō (“beginning, source, origin”), equivalent to origin + -al; see origin.
column3: adjective. Relating to the origin or beginning; preceding all others.

column2: From Late Middle English orthodoxe, from Middle French orthodoxe and its etymon Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”). Displaced native Old English wuldorlīċ.
column3: adjective. Conforming to the accepted, established, or traditional doctrines of a given faith, religion, or ideology.

column2: From outdate + -ed.
column3: adjective. Out of date, old-fashioned, antiquated.

column2: From outgo + -ing, out + going.
column3: adjective. Extroverted: talkative, friendly, and social, especially with respect to meeting new people easily and comfortably; outgiving.

column2: From Middle English outright. By surface analysis, out + right.
column3: adverb. Wholly; completely; entirely.

column2: From out- + weigh.
column3: verb. To exceed in weight or mass.

column2: Inherited from Middle English overcomen, inherited from Old English ofercuman (“to overcome, subdue, compel, conquer, obtain, attain, reach, overtake”). By surface analysis, over- + come. Cognate with Dutch overkomen, German überkommen, Danish overkomme, Swedish överkomma.
column3: verb. To surmount (a physical or abstract obstacle); to prevail over, to get the better of.

column2: From Middle English overflowen, from Old English oferflōwan, equivalent to over- + flow.
column3: noun. The spillage resultant from overflowing.

column2: From Middle English owerheved, over-hed, over hede (adverb), from Old English oferhēafod (adverb), equivalent to over- + head. Compare German Low German overhoopt, överhoopt, German überhaupt. Piecewise doublet of overchief.
column3: adjective. Located above, especially over the head.

column2: From over- + load.
column3: verb. To load excessively.

column2: From over- + long.
column3: adjective. Too long; overly long.

column2: Inherited from Middle English overloken. From Middle English overloken; equivalent to over- + look.
column3: noun. A vista or point that gives a view down toward something else.

column2: From Middle English overriden, from Old English oferrīdan, equivalent to over- + ride. Cognate with Dutch overrijden, German überreiten, Danish override.
column3: verb. To ride across or beyond something.

column2: From earlier oversea, equivalent to oversea + -s. Compare West Frisian oerseesk, Dutch overzees, German Übersee, Danish oversøisk.
column3: adjective. Abroad, especially across the sea.

column2: From over- + time.
column3: noun. Working time outside of one's regular hours.

column2: From over- + tone, calque of German Oberton.
column3: noun. A tone whose frequency is an integer multiple of another; a member of the harmonic series.

column2: From over- + view.
column3: noun. A brief summary, as of a book or a presentation.

column2: From pacify + -er.
column3: noun. Someone or something that pacifies.

column2: From Middle English paynles, peynlees, equivalent to pain + -less. Compare West Frisian pynleas (“painless”), Dutch pijnloos (“painless”).
column3: adjective. Free from pain; without pain or trouble.

column2: By surface analysis, paint + -ing.
column3: noun. An illustration or artwork done with the use of paint.

column2: From Middle English paradis, paradise, paradys, from Late Old English paradīs, borrowed from Old French paradis, from Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah. Doublet of parvis. Displaced Old English neorxnawang.
column3: noun. The place where sanctified souls are believed to live after death.

column2: From Middle French parallèle and its etymon Latin parallēlus, parallēlos. The verb is from the noun. See also para- and allo-.
column3: adjective. Equally distant from one another at all points.

column2: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek παράνοια (paránoia, “madness”), from παράνοος (paránoos, “demented”), from παρά (pará, “beyond, beside”) + νόος (nóos, “mind, spirit”). By surface analysis, para- (“abnormal, beyond”) + nous (“mind”) + -ia (“(medical) condition”).
column3: noun. A psychotic disorder, now called delusional disorder, often (in one of six subtypes) characterized by delusions of persecution and a perceived threat against the individual affected with the disorder, and often associated with false accusations and a general mistrust of others.

column2: From paranoia + -oid.
column3: adjective. Of, related to, or suffering from clinical paranoia.

column2: From Middle French particule, and its source, Latin particula (“small part, particle”), diminutive of pars (“part, piece”). Semantically displaced native Old English grot whence modern English groat.
column3: noun. A very small piece of matter, a fragment; especially, the smallest possible part of something.

column2: From French passeport, from passer (“pass”) + port (“port”). Compare portpass. Equivalent to pass + port.
column3: noun. An official document normally used for international journeys, which proves the identity and nationality of the person for whom it was issued.

column2: From pass + word. The sentry-passing sense predates the cryptographic sense and was its inspiration.
column3: noun. A word relayed to a person to gain admittance to a place or to gain access to information.

column2: From Middle French pathétique, from Latin patheticus, from Ancient Greek παθητικός (pathētikós, “subject to feeling, capable of feeling, impassioned”), from παθητός (pathētós, “one who has suffered, subject to suffering”), from πάσχω (páskhō, “to suffer”). By surface analysis, path- + -etic.
column3: adjective. Arousing pity, sympathy, or compassion; exciting pathos.

column2: Inherited from Middle English pacience, from Old French pacience (modern French patience), from Latin patientia (“suffering; endurance, patience”), from patiens, present active participle of patior (“suffer, experience, wait”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hurt”). Displaced Old English ġeþyld.
column3: noun. The quality of being patient.

column2: From Middle English pament, from Anglo-Norman pavement and reinforced by Middle French pavement; both from Latin pavīmentum (“paved surface or floor”), from pavīre (“to beat, to ram, to tread down”). Morphologically pave + -ment.
column3: noun. A paved surface; a hard covering on the ground.

column2: From Middle English peesful, pesful, paisful, pesefull. By surface analysis, peace + -ful. Displaced native Old English friþsum.
column3: adjective. Not at war; not disturbed by strife or turmoil.

column2: From Latin pecūliāris (“one's own”), from pecūlium (“private property”), from pecus (“cattle”).
column3: adjective. Out of the ordinary; odd; strange; unusual.

column2: From pedant + -ic.
column3: adjective. Being overly concerned with formal rules and trivial points of learning, like a pedant.

column2: From Italian pedanteria, equivalent to pedant + -ry. Compare also French pédanterie.
column3: noun. An excessive attention to detail or rules. An instance of such behaviour.

column2: From Middle English perceyven, borrowed from Old French percevoir, perceveir, from Latin percipiō, past participle perceptus (“take hold of, obtain, receive, observe”), from per (“by, through”) + capiō (“to take”); see capable. Compare conceive, deceive, receive.
column3: verb. To become aware of, through the physical senses, to see; to understand.

column2: From French périodique, from Medieval Latin periodicus (“cyclical”), from Latin periodus (“complete sentence, period, circuit”), from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos, “cycle, period of time”). By surface analysis, period + -ic.
column3: adjective. Relative to a period or periods.

column2: From Middle English personal, personele, from Anglo-Norman personel, personal, personell, Old French personal, personel, from Late Latin persōnālis (“of a person, personly”), equivalent to person + -al. Doublet of personnel.
column3: adjective. Pertaining to persons (human beings as opposed to things or animals).

column2: From Latin persuādeō (“to persuade”). Cognate to for, sweet.
column3: verb. To successfully convince (someone) to agree to, accept, or do something, usually through reasoning and verbal influence.

column2: From Middle English perverse, pervers, from Old French pervers, from Latin perversum (“thoroughly turned”), past participle of pervertere, from per- (“thoroughly”) + vertere (“to turn”).
column3: adjective. Turned aside while against something, splitting off from a thing.

column2: From Middle English pharmacy, borrowed from Middle French pharmacie (“the art of creating drugs; a drug, especially a laxative”), from Old French farmacie, from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”), from φάρμακον (phármakon, “a drug, charm, enchantment”), of uncertain but likely Pre-Greek origin. Attested since late 14th century.
column3: noun. A place where prescription drugs are sold or dispensed.

column2: Borrowed from Late Latin physicālis, from Latin physica (“study of nature”), from Ancient Greek φυσική (phusikḗ), feminine singular of φυσικός (phusikós, “natural; physical”), from φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth; nature, quality; form, shape; type, kind”), from φῠ́ω (phŭ́ō, “grow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to appear, become, rise up”).
column3: adjective. Of medicine. Pertaining to the field of medicine; medical. That practises medicine; pertaining to doctors, physicianly. Medicinal; good for the health, curative, therapeutic.

column2: From pipe + line.
column3: noun. A conduit made of pipes used to convey water, gas or petroleum, etc.

column2: From Middle French plateforme (“a flat form”), from plate (“flat”) (from Old French plat, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “flat”)) + forme (“form”) (from Latin fōrma (“shape; figure; form”)); compare flatscape.
column3: noun. A raised stage from which speeches are made and on which musical and other performances are made.

column2: From Middle English plesaunte, from Old French plaisant. By surface analysis, please + -ant. Related to Dutch plezant (“full of fun or pleasure”). Partly displaced Old English wynsum, which became Modern English winsome.
column3: adjective. Giving pleasure; pleasing in manner.

column2: From Middle English plesynge, pleizinge, plesende (present participle), equivalent to please + -ing.
column3: adjective. Agreeable; giving pleasure, cheer, enjoyment or gratification.

column2: From Early Modern English pleasur, plesur, alteration (with ending accommodated to -ure) of Middle English plaisir (“pleasure”), from Old French plesir, plaisir (“to please”), infinitive used as a noun, conjugated form of plaisir or plaire, from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Proto-Indo-European * pleh₂-k - (“wide and flat”). Related to Dutch plezier (“pleasure, fun”). More at please.
column3: noun. A state of being pleased or contented; gratification.

column2: From point + -ing.
column3: noun. The action of the verb to point.

column2: From the adjective politic, by analogy with Aristotle’s τά πολῑτῐκᾱ́ (tá polītĭkā́, “affairs of state”).
column3: noun. A methodology and activities associated with the interpersonal aspects of running a government, an organization, or a movement.

column2: Borrowed from Middle French populace, from Italian popolaccio, from popolo + -accio (“pejorative suffix”), from Latin populus.
column3: noun. The common people of a nation.

column2: Borrowed from Medieval Latin populātus, past participle of populor (“populate”), from Latin populus (“people”).
column3: verb. To supply with inhabitants; to people.

column2: From Middle English portable, from Middle French portable and Latin portābilis. By surface analysis, port (“to carry”) + -able.
column3: adjective. Able to be carried or easily moved.

column2: From Middle English posicioun, from Old French posicion, from Latin positiō (“a putting, position”), from positus (“placed, situated”), past participle of pōnō (“to place”); see ponent. Compare apposition, composition, deposition; see pose.
column3: noun. A place or location.

column2: From Old French positif, from Latin positivus, from the past participle stem of ponere (“to place”). Compare posit.
column3: adjective. Included, present, characterized by affirmation.

column2: From Middle English possible, from Old French possible, from Latin possibilis (“possible”), from posse, possum (“to be able”); see power. Displaced Middle English acumendlic (“possible”), from Old English ācumendlīċ (“possible”). Compare also Old English mihtelīċ (“strong, capable, powerful, possible”), which was cognate with Old High German mahtlīh (“possible”) and Old Norse máttulígr (“mighty, possible”). Compare also Dutch mogelijk (“possible”) and German möglich (“possible”).
column3: adjective. Able but not certain to happen; neither inevitable nor impossible.

column2: From possible + -ly.
column3: adverb. Perhaps; indicates that the proposition may be true (is not certainly false) regardless of any facts or circumstances known to, stated by or implied by the speaker.

column2: From post + card.
column3: noun. A rectangular piece of thick paper or thin cardboard, typically used for sending messages by mail without the need for an envelope.

column2: From Latin postpōnō (“to put after; to postpone”) from post (“after”) + pōnō (“to put; to place”), compare forestall.
column3: verb. To delay or put off an event, appointment, etc.

column2: From Middle English pouerful, powarfull. By surface analysis, power + -ful.
column3: adjective. Having, or capable of exerting, power or influence.

column2: The noun is from Middle English practice, practique, practyse, from the verb; also compare Medieval Latin prāctica.. Displaced native Old English sidu. The verb is from Middle English practice, practise, practize, practyse, from Middle French pratiser, practiser, alteration of practiquer, from Medieval Latin prācticāre, from Late Latin prācticus, from Ancient Greek πρακτικός (praktikós). The spelling practice is attested once in Middle English for both the noun and the verb. The noun began to be assimilated in spelling to nouns in -ice; practise (noun) is now obsolete.
column3: noun. Repetition of an activity to improve a skill.

column2: Inherited from Middle English precious, borrowed from Old French precios (“valuable, costly, precious, beloved, also affected, finical”), from Latin pretiōsus (“of great value, costly, dear, precious”), from pretium (“value, price”); see price.
column3: adjective. Of high value or worth.

column2: From Middle English preignant, from Old French preignant, pregnant, also prenant (compare archaic Modern French prégnant), and their source, Latin praegnāns (“pregnant”), probably from prae- (“pre-”) + *gnāscī, an archaic form of nāscī (“to be born”). Displaced Old English bearnēacen (literally "child-enlarged").
column3: adjective. Carrying developing offspring within the body.

column2: See premise
column3: noun. plural of premise

column2: From prepare + -ed.
column3: adjective. Disposed, willing, ready (to do something).

column2: Through Old French presence, from Latin praesentia (“a being present”), from praesentem. Displaced native Old English andweardnes.
column3: noun. The fact or condition of being present, or of being within sight or call, or at hand.

column2: From Middle English preserven, from Old French preserver, from Medieval Latin prēservāre (“keep, preserve”), from Late Latin praeservāre (“guard beforehand”), from prae (“before”, adverb) + servāre (“maintain, keep”). Displaced native Old English nerian.
column3: noun. A sweet spread made of any of a variety of fruits.

column2: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from pressing.
column3: adjective. Needing urgent attention.

column2: From Latin pressūra.
column3: noun. A pressing; a force applied to a surface.

column2: From Latin praevius.
column3: adjective. Prior; occurring before something else, either in time or order.

column2: By surface analysis, print + -ing.
column3: noun. The process or business of producing printed material by means of inked type and a printing press or similar technology.

column2: Deverbal from print out.
column3: noun. Something printed on paper, usually a copy generated by a printer (machine).

column2: From Old French priorite, from Latin priōritās. Surface analysis: prior + -ity.
column3: noun. An item's relative importance.

column2: From Middle English prisoner, from Old French prisonier (compare Medieval Latin prisōnārius), equivalent to prison + -er.
column3: noun. A person incarcerated in a prison, while on trial or serving a sentence.

column2: From Middle English probable, from Old French probable, from Latin probābilis (“that may be proved, credible”), from probāre (“to test, examine”); see probe, probity, prove. Compare recent doublet provable.
column3: adjective. Likely or most likely to be true.

column2: From Middle English probably, probabily, equivalent to probable + -ly.
column3: adverb. In all likelihood.

column2: From Middle English proclamen, proclaime, from Old French proclamer, from Latin prōclāmō, prōclāmāre, from prō- (“forth”) + clāmō (“to shout, cry out”). Spelling altered by influence of claim, from the same Latin source (clāmō).
column3: verb. To announce or declare.

column2: From produce + -er.
column3: noun. An individual or organization that creates goods and services.

column2: From Middle English profound, profounde, from Anglo-Norman profound, from Old French profont, profonde, from Latin profundus (“deep, profound”), from prō + fundus (“bottom; foundation”).
column3: adjective. Descending far below the surface; opening or reaching to great depth; deep.

column2: From Middle English progresse, from Old French progres (“a going forward”), from Latin prōgressus (“an advance”), from the participle stem of prōgredī (“to go forward, advance, develop”), from pro- (“forth, before”) + gradi (“to walk, go”). Displaced native Old English forþgang.
column3: noun. Movement or advancement through a series of events, or points in time; development through time.

column2: From Middle English prohibiten, from Latin prohibeō (“to fend off, prevent, prohibit”) (through past participle prohibitus).
column3: verb. To forbid, disallow, or proscribe officially; to make illegal or illicit.

column2: From prompt + -ly.
column3: adverb. In a prompt manner. Both soon and quickly. Exactly at a specific time.

column2: From proper + -ly.
column3: adverb. In a proper manner, appropriately, suitably; correctly, justifiably

column2: From Middle English propertee, properte, propirte, proprete, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Old French propreté, proprieté (“propriety, fitness, property”), from Latin proprietās (“a peculiarity, one's peculiar nature or quality, right or fact of possession, property”), from proprius (“special, particular, one's own”). Equivalent to proper + -ty. Doublet of propriety.
column3: noun. Something that is owned.

column2: From propose + -al.
column3: noun. Something which is proposed, or offered for consideration or acceptance.

column2: From Middle English prospecte, from Latin prōspectus (“view, sight, prospect; panorama”), from prōspiciō (“to look forward”) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns), from pro (“before, forward”) + speciō, spiciō (“to look, to see”). By surface analysis, pro- + -spect. Doublet of prospectus and prospekt. The verb is from the noun.
column3: noun. The region which the eye overlooks at one time; a view; a scene; an outlook.

column2: Borrowed from Middle French protocolle, protocole (“document, record”), from Late Latin protocollum (“the first sheet of a volume (on which contents and errata were written)”), from Byzantine Greek πρωτόκολλον (prōtókollon, “first sheet glued onto a manuscript”), from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”) + κόλλα (kólla, “glue”).
column3: noun. The minutes, or official record, of a negotiation or transaction; especially a document drawn up officially which forms the legal basis for subsequent agreements based on it.

column2: From public + -ly.
column3: adverb. In public, openly, in an open and public manner.

column2: From punch + -ing.
column3: noun. gerund of punch An incident in which someone is punched. The process of making holes in something (for example, a leather belt or a rail ticket).

column2: Borrowed from Late Latin punctūra.
column3: noun. The act or an instance of puncturing.

column2: From Middle English purchasen, from Anglo-Norman purchacer (“seek to obtain”) from pur- (from Latin pro-) + chac(i)er (“to chase, pursue”). Compare Old French porchacier (“to follow, to chase”), which has given French pourchasser (“to chase without relent”).
column3: noun. The acquisition of title to, or property in, anything for a price; buying for money or its equivalent.

column2: From Middle English quantite, from Old French quantité, from Latin quantitās (“quantity”), from quantus (“how much”).
column3: noun. A fundamental, generic term used when referring to the measurement (count, amount) of a scalar, vector, number of items or to some other way of denominating the value of a collection or group of items.

column2: From Middle English questioun, from Anglo-Norman questiun, from Old French question, from Latin quaestiōnem, accusative of quaestiō (“a seeking, investigation, inquiry, question”), from quaerere (“to seek, ask, inquire”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”). Doublet of quest. Partially displaced native Old English āscung, whence asking. Compare also Middle Low German quēstie (“questioning; inquiry”), Middle High German questje (“question”).
column3: noun. A worded or expressed sentence, phrase, or only a word on its own, which asks for information, a reply, or a response; an interrogative.

column2: From rail + road.
column3: noun. A permanent track consisting of fixed metal rails to drive trains or similar motorized vehicles on.

column2: From random + -ly.
column3: adverb. In a random manner.

column2: From Old French rationel, rational, from Latin rationalis (“of or belonging to reason, rational, reasonable; having a ratio”), from ratio (“reason; calculation”).
column3: adjective. Capable of reasoning.

column2: From Middle English reching, rechyng, recchinge, rechand, from Old English *rǣċende and reċċende (“reaching”), from Proto-Germanic *raikijandz, present participle of *raikijaną (“to stretch, reach”) and Proto-Germanic *rakjandz, present participle of *rakjaną (“to stretch, straighten”). Equivalent to reach + -ing.
column3: verb. present participle and gerund of reach

column2: Inherited from Middle English reaccion, from Old French reaction, from Latin reāctiō, from the verb reagō, from re- (“again”) + agō (“to act”); more at re-, action; equivalent to react + -ion.
column3: noun. An action or statement in response to a stimulus or other event.

column2: From read + -able.
column3: adjective. Legible, possible to read or at least decipher.

column2: From Old French rasseürer (French rassurer), from re- + asseürer; as if re- + assure.
column3: verb. To assure anew; to restore confidence to; to free from fear or self-doubt.

column2: Inherited from Middle English receyvour, from Anglo-Norman receverre, receivour et al., later also reformed as receive + -er. Compare recevor, rescaivour.
column3: noun. A person who receives. An official whose job is to receive taxes or other monies; a tax collector, a treasurer. A person who receives something in a general sense; a recipient. A person who accepts stolen goods. A person or company appointed to settle the affairs of an insolvent entity.

column2: From recent + -ly.
column3: adverb. In the recent past

column2: From Middle English rekles, reckeles, rekkeles, (also recheles), from Old English rēcelēas (“reckless, careless, negligent”), equivalent to reck + -less. Cognate with West Frisian roekeleas (“reckless”), Dutch roekeloos (“reckless”), German Low German ruuklos (“careless”), German ruchlos (“careless, notorious”).
column3: adjective. Careless or heedless; headstrong or rash.

column2: From Middle English recordour, borrowed from Old French recordour, from Old French recordeor, from Medieval Latin recordātor, from Latin recordor (“call to mind, remember, recollect”), from re- (“back, again”) + cor (“heart; mind”). By surface analysis, record + -er.
column3: noun. An apparatus for recording; a device which records.

column2: From recover + -y, from Middle English recoveree, from Old French recovree, from recovrer (“recover”).
column3: noun. The act or process of regaining or repossession of something lost. A clever verbal solution to an embarrassing verbal mistake.

column2: From re- + define.
column3: verb. To define again or differently. To give a new or different definition to (a word). To define a previously defined area of storage etc. in a different manner, e.g. changing it from textual to numeric.

column2: From re- + direct.
column3: verb. To give new direction to; to change the course, direction or destination of.

column2: From re- + format.
column3: verb. To format anew or again, generally erasing a previous format.

column2: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
column3: verb. simple past and past participle of regard

column2: From Middle French régional, from Latin regiōnālis.
column3: adjective. Of, or pertaining to, a specific region or district.

column2: From Medieval Latin registrum, from Late Latin regesta (“list, items recorded”), from Latin regerō (“to record, to carry back”), from re- + gerō (“to carry, bear”). Compare Latin registoria (“a treasurer”). Some senses influenced by association with unrelated Latin regō (“to rule”).
column3: noun. A formal recording of names, events, transactions, etc.

column2: From Middle English relacion, relacioun, from Anglo-Norman relacioun and Old French relacion (whence French relation), from Latin relātiō, noun of process form from perfect passive participle relātus (“related”), from verb referō (“to refer, to relate”), from prefix re- (“again”) + ferō (“to bear, to carry”). By surface analysis, relate + -ion. Doublet of relazione.
column3: noun. The manner in which two things may be associated.

column2: From Middle French relatif, from Late Latin relātīvus, from Latin relātus, perfect passive participle of referō (“to carry back, to ascribe”), from re- (“again”) + ferō (“to bear or carry”). By surface analysis, relate + -ive.
column3: adjective. Connected to or depending on something else; comparative.

column2: From Scots relevant meaning "legally pertinent," used in Scottish legal circles starting in the early 1500s, and first used in English in the 1700s. Borrowed from Latin relevāns, relevāntem, present active participle of relevō (“lift up again, lighten, relieve”), from re- (“again”) + levō (“lift”).
column3: adjective. Related, connected, or pertinent to a topic. Directly related, connected, or pertinent, with important ramifications or implications.

column2: From rely + -able.
column3: adjective. Suitable or fit to be relied on; worthy of dependence, reliance or trust; dependable, trustworthy

column2: From reliable + -ly.
column3: adverb. In a reliable manner.

column2: From Middle English religioun, from Old French religion, from Latin religiō (“scrupulousness, pious misgivings, superstition, conscientiousness, sanctity, an object of veneration, cult-observance, reverence”). Most likely from the Proto-Indo-European *h₂leg- with the meanings preserved in Latin dīligere and legere (“to read repeatedly”, “to have something solely in mind”). Displaced Old English ǣfæstnes (“religion, lawfulness”).
column3: noun. Belief in a spiritual or metaphysical reality (often including at least one deity), accompanied by practices or rituals pertaining to the belief.

column2: From Middle English remembren, from Old French remembrer (“to remember”), from Late Latin rememorari (“to remember again”), from re- + memor (“mindful”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-, *(s)mer- (“to think about, be mindful, remember”). Cognate with Old English mimorian, mymerian (“to remember, commemorate”), Old English māmorian (“to deliberate, plan out, design”). More at mimmer and mammer. Compare also dialectical English umbethink. The success of the Old French word was helped by its proximity in sound and meaning to an existing Germanic word: Old English mimorian, mymerian (“to remember, commemorate”) from Proto-Germanic *mimrōną, *mīmrōną (“to remember, be mindful”), from the same Indo-European source, and is akin to Saterland Frisian miemerje (“to ponder, reflect”), Middle Low German mimeren (“to ponder, meditate”), Middle Dutch mimeren (“to reflect, think to oneself”) (Dutch mijmeren (“to muse, reflect deeply”)), Old English ġemimor (“mindful”), Old Norse Mímir, Mim (“Norse god of memory”), Old English māmrian (“to think out, design”). Related to mourn. Displaced native Middle English ȝemuneȝen (“to remember”), from Old English ġemynegian (“to remember, remind”); Middle English minnen (“to remember, have in mind”), from Old Norse minna (“to remind”); Middle English munden, ȝemunden (“to bear in mind, remember”), from Old English ġemynd (“memory, remembrance”); Middle English ithenchen, ȝethenchen (“to think on, remember”), from Old English ġeþencan; Middle English manien (“to remind, mention, remember”), from Old English manian (“to admonish, remind, mention”).
column3: verb. To recall from one's memory; to have an image in one's memory.

column2: From remind + -er.
column3: noun. Someone or something that reminds.

column2: From remote + -ly.
column3: adverb. At a distance, far away.

column2: From re- + phrase.
column3: verb. To say or write something with different wording.

column2: From Middle English reportour, from Old French reporteur; equivalent to report + -er.
column3: noun. Someone or something that reports.

column2: Early Modern French rechercher (“to examine closely”), from Old French recerchier (“to seek, to look for”), by surface analysis, re- + search.
column3: noun. Diligent inquiry or examination to seek or revise facts, principles, theories, applications, etc. (that are currently available, or that are familiar to one's self).

column2: From Middle English resemblen, from Anglo-Norman resembler, ressembler, from re- + sembler (“to seem”). By surface analysis, re- + semble.
column3: verb. To be like or similar to (something); to represent as similar.

column2: From Middle English resident, from Anglo-Norman resident, from Latin residēns, present participle of resideō (“to remain behind, reside, dwell”), equivalent to reside + -ent, from re- (“back”) + sedeō (“to sit”). Doublet of resiant and rezident. The espionage sense is a semantic loan from Russian резиде́нт (rezidént). (physician): So called because in the 19th century they resided in the hospital dormitories.
column3: noun. A person, animal or plant living at a certain location or in a certain area.
